Sentinel-2 metrics indicated a shorter growing season – later SOS (5 days for Fagus sylvatica ; 3 days for Picea abies ) and earlier EOS (13 days for Fagus sylvatica ). Despite these offsets, satellite data captured similar annual and regional trends. POS closely tracked SOS trends, but offered more reliable sampling opportunities due to more stable vegetation conditions and typically lower cloud cover during summer. Satellite-derived EOS may reflect stress responses missed by ground observations. Elevation trends also differed, with in situ data showing steeper slopes of the SOS-elevation relationships. Limitations of satellite data remained in mountainous regions due to topography and cloud cover, limiting sampling sizes. Overall, satellite remote sensing can complement in situ observations by facilitating observations across large geographic and temporal domains. In contrast, in situ observations provide long-term historical data unaffected by atmospheric conditions or possible technical issues of satellites. • Phenology metrics for beech and spruce derived from satellite remote sensing. • Comprehensive comparison of in situ and Sentinel-2 species phenology metrics. • Analyzing interannual and regional patterns of phenology between data sources. • Assessing the influence of elevation and topographic wetness on phenology metrics. • Discussing how satellite remote sensing can support conventional phenology monitoring.

title: Diversity of fishes in karst Plateau lakes, Guizhou, China
abstract: • Marked spatial heterogeneity in fish community assembly across karst plateau lakes. • Contrasting assembly processes: Stochasticity dominates in Baihua and Wanfeng Lakes, determinism in Hongfeng Lake. • Water quality indirectly shapes assembly via modulating network stability. • Novel integration of eDNA, network analysis, and SEM for community ecology. Exploring fish community structure and assembly mechanisms across multiple ecological scales is crucial for understanding the sustainable management of lake ecosystems. This study focused on a typical karst plateau lake in Southwest China, including Baihua Lake, Hongfeng Lake and Wanfeng Lake. integrating eDNA high-throughput sequencing, network topology analysis, and structural equation modeling to systematically analyze the spatial patterns, assembly processes, and environmental responses of the fish community. The results demonstrate that fish species diversity exhibits significant spatial heterogeneity. Multiple lines of evidence, including the neutral model, ecological niche width, and βNTI collectively indicate that stochastic processes predominantly govern the assembly of fish communities, particularly in Baihua Lake and Wanfeng Lake. In contrast, deterministic factors such as environmental filtering and spatial constraints play a more prominent role in Hongfeng Lake. Analyses of distance decay and environmental factors further reveal that the relationship between community similarity, geographical distance, and environmental heterogeneity varies significantly across regions. Molecular ecological network analysis reveals that Hongfeng Lake exhibits the largest network scale and highest stability, which supports the maintenance of biodiversity. The structural equation model demonstrates that water quality directly influences community assembly by regulating the molecular ecological network, while assembly exerts a negative regulatory effect on network stability. The overall model shows a high goodness-of-fit (GoF = 0.74), and core path relationships were statistically significant. This study elucidates the multidimensional assembly mechanisms of fish communities in karst lakes and the regulatory interactions within the network, providing novel insights and a theoretical foundation for the management and restoration of biodiversity in high-altitude lake ecosystems.

title: Dominant role of stand structure in biomass carbon storage of subtropical natural Quercus forests in South China
abstract: • Stand structure has a dominant effect on carbon storage of natural Quercus forests. • Interactions Interaction between stand structure factors, environmental factors, and the two factors themselves affects the carbon storage of natural Quercus forests. • Stand structure factors affecting the carbon storage capacity of natural Quercus forests have specific ecological thresholds. Forest carbon sequestration plays a crucial role in mitigating climate change. Understanding the mechanisms driving biomass carbon storage of subtropical natural Quercus forests is vital for improving their carbon sequestration capacity. This study examined 170 natural Quercus forest plots in Hunan Province, a subtropical region of China, to elucidate the regulatory influence of stand structure and environmental factors on forest carbon storage, including aboveground, belowground, and total forest carbon storage. We systematically gathered plot data and employed Spearman’s correlation analysis, machine learning method, SHAP analysis, and threshold analysis to quantify the contributions and interaction effects of stand structure and environmental factors, identifying the threshold ranges of key determinants. The Spearman’s correlation results revealed that stand structure shows an overall positive relationship with forest carbon storage. However, the machine learning (XGBoost) and SHAP analysis further demonstrated that this impact is nonlinear and stage-dependent, accompanied by distinct threshold effects. The findings demonstrate that stand structural attributes explain over 90 % of the variation in forest carbon storage. Key drivers include mean diameter at breast height (13.54–13.86 cm), stand density (1082–2407 trees hm −2 ), age, tree height, stand layering, and Quercus basal area ratio, exhibiting significant threshold effects. Additionally, second-order interactions among stand structure factors, environmental factors, and between the two categories exert important influences on forest carbon storage dynamics. The research concludes that stand structure is pivotal in regulating forest carbon storage in subtropical natural Quercus forests. Identifying its threshold offers a precise foundation for forest management, enhances the understanding of forest carbon sink mechanisms, and provides scientific support for achieving carbon neutrality in forest management.

title: Attribution of runoff and sediment changes in the Wuding River Basin based on the Budyko-Kaya framework
abstract: Attribution analysis of runoff and sediment evolution, driven by the combined effects of climate change and human activities, remains a critical and complex challenge in contemporary hydrological research. This study integrated the Budyko elasticity method and the Kaya identity to quantify the contributions of climatic factors and underlying surface conditions to runoff and sediment changes, and to examine their spatial sensitivities and attribution differences. The results revealed significant declining trends in both runoff and sediment, with abrupt regime shifts identified in 1996 for runoff and in 2002 for sediment. The reduction in runoff was notably more pronounced. Runoff exhibited dominant periodicities of 41, 24, 12, and 5 a, while sediment displayed cycles of 47, 21, and 5 a. During the runoff change period, spatial heterogeneity in dominant driving factors was evident: underlying surface changes played a leading role in the upstream and central regions, whereas precipitation was the primary driver in the downstream areas. Across the entire basin, the contributions of m , P , and E 0 to runoff changes were 65 %, 27.9 %, and 7.1 %, respectively. During the sediment change period, C (45.9 %) and m (32.8 %) were the dominant factors, while the influences of P (18.2 %) and E 0 (3.1 %) were relatively minor. Following the regime shifts, increases in P , E 0 , and m significantly influenced the evolution of runoff-sediment synchronicity. Enhanced precipitation led to asynchronous responses between runoff and sediment. Underlying surface factors affected the coupling relationship by modulating runoff generation and erosion, while potential evapotranspiration exerted contrasting effects on synchronicity across different periods. The study further revealed that precipitation was the dominant climatic driver of runoff and sediment dynamics, while the underlying surface modulated its influence pathways. Oceanic factors influenced periodic fluctuations in runoff and sediment by altering atmospheric circulation patterns. Regional soil and water conservation measures have effectively reduced runoff and sediment intensity, while evolving land use patterns have enhanced the basin’s regulatory capacity.

title: Spatiotemporal coupling mechanism between land use and water disaster risk in lake-dominated basins: a multimodel assessment of the Dongting Lake Basin
Regional adaptability and integrated evaluation of saline-alkali soil remediation technologies: a comprehensive review
Social value-weighted greenspace exposure index: A novel metric integrating cultural ecosystem services for equitable benefits
abstract: Well-maintained urban greenspace (UGS) can provide benefits for human health and recreation. Existing evaluations often focus solely on greenspace presence, overlooking their attractiveness and the resulting quality as perceived by the citizens. Thereby, we lack comprehensive understanding on whether citizens have equal access to high-quality UGS that can truly provide health benefits and enhance life satisfaction, obscuring systemic inequalities in environmental justice. Here we sought to address this challenge by taking cultural ecosystem service (CES) and social values of UGS as a proxy for the perceived UGS quality. Through a four-month survey of 558 residents in Xiamen, China, we quantified UGS social values and integrated them into the evaluations of UGS use and the inequalities therein between neighborhoods. Our findings indicate that previous metrics may misrepresent actual enjoyment of UGS (with coverage-based valuation at 10.28% while social value-weighted assessment is 6.49%), typically because neighborhoods may have greenspaces with disparate social values, causing an unbalanced distribution of attractive UGSs. When combined with major inequalities in access to high-quality UGS, this may cause significant differences in perceived health benefits among citizens (Gini coefficient increases from 0.69 to 0.79). We additionally observed that the three focal drivers of these inequalities—greenspace coverage, local population mobility and UGS social values—vary across neighborhoods, informing targeted policy interventions. We highlight that disparities in UGS social values contribute to major extents to inequalities in health benefits, emphasizing the need to extend greenspace assessments from quantity to quality and ensuring equal access to high-quality greenspaces and their well-being benefits.

title: Basin characteristics determine longitudinal distribution and source composition of nitrogen pollution in a multi-tributary mountain river basin
abstract: Longitudinal distribution and source identification of nitrogen pollution are important for the basin delicacy management and pollution source control. The upstream Hanjiang River Basin was divided into 95 sub-basins based on topography, then 190 riverine water samples in two seasons and end-member samples of nitrate pollution sources were collected to conduct a spatial analysis of various forms of riverine nitrogen and source composition of nitrate along the river course. The concentrations among ammonium nitrogen, nitrate nitrogen and nitrate nitrogen isotope in the mainstream gradually increased from the headwater to riverine sections of Hanzhong City and the Huangjinxia Reservoir. However, concentrations did not increase continuously from the Huangjinxia Reservoir but fluctuated until the river entered the estuary in Danjiangkou Reservoir. Results of MixSIAR in April and August indicated that cropland contributed nearly 50% of the nitrate, while the contribution rates of both wastewater and forest & grassland ranged from 20% to 30%. Results of the random forests model and structural equation modeling showed that basin characteristics indirectly affected the distribution of nitrate sources by directly influencing land uses and human activities. Watershed area, perimeter and total length of river network were positively correlated with the contribution rate of wastewater, while altitude and slope were positively correlated with the contribution rate of cropland and forest & grassland because basin characteristics such as topography, slope and altitude influenced land uses by affecting human activities. This study provided insight for understanding the cumulative and changing process of nitrate pollution along the course of rivers.

title: Water footprint of China’s coal mining sector substantially underestimated
abstract: China grapples with severe water scarcity exacerbated by a pronounced reverse spatial distribution between coal and water resources. Accurately assessing the water footprint of the coal mining is crucial for quantifying the water-associated risks and guiding sustainable sector practices. However, existing studies lack systematic frameworks for integrating grey water footprint accounting of heavy metals and other pollutants, leading to underestimated impacts. Based on the data of 12,378 coal mines operated from 2013 to 2022 in China, this study establishes a comprehensive water footprint assessment framework, integrating multiple spatial analysis, long temporal trends, and dual production-consumption perspectives. The results indicate that 208 coal mining technological configurations exhibit water footprint intensities ranging from 3.16 to 33.44 m3/t, with grey water contributing more than 85%. Large-surface coal mines demonstrate the lowest intensity, validating their water-saving potential. Over the decade, the water footprint intensity of coal production in China has decreased by 17.76%, while the consumption-side decreased by 16.75%. The total water footprint for coal production and consumption approximately fell from 43.5 Gm3 in 2013 to 38 Gm3 in 2022. Inter-provincial virtual water flows predominantly follow a north-to-south and west-to-east pattern, peaking in Shanxi-Hebei transfers exceeding 1 Gm3. Technological advancements reduced the national total consumption water footprint by 7.99 Gm3, whereas supply chain optimization drove more significant reductions in Fujian, Hunan, Jiangxi, and Chongqing. By rectifying grey water footprint underestimation and emphasizing heavy metal control, this study provides a scientific foundation of coal mining sector for spatially targeted water governance and ecological restoration.

title: Divergence in global plant carbon use efficiency across data-driven estimates, satellite product, and process-oriented models
abstract: • High-latitude CUE patterns diverge, with the data-driven showing lower values. • CUE trends vary: MODIS up, the data-driven down, DGVMs show no clear change. • Mean annual temperature mainly drives CUE, with method-specific effects. Plant carbon use efficiency (CUE)—the proportion of net to gross primary productivity (NPP/GPP)—is a critical indicator of terrestrial carbon cycling, yet its global patterns and trends remain uncertain due to challenges in directly measuring carbon flux. Here, we compared global plant CUE estimates using three methods: (1) a data-driven estimate derived from existing GPP, ecosystem respiration and soil heterotrophic respiration datasets (hereafter referred to as data-driven CUE), (2) MODIS satellite product, and (3) dynamic global vegetation models (DGVMs). We found significant spatial and temporal divergences in CUE emerged among the three methods. Specially, the data-driven method showed lower CUE in northern high latitudes and higher CUE in sub-Saharan Africa, India, and northern Australia, while MODIS and DGVM estimates exhibited opposing patterns. Temporally, MODIS data indicated a global CUE increase during 2001–2012, data-driven method suggested a decline, and most DGVMs showed no significant trend. Machine learning-based spatial attribution showed that mean annual temperature primarily drove spatial CUE variability among the three approaches, with method-specific relationships. These discrepancies underscore the need to reconcile methodological biases to enhance the accuracy of global plant CUE mapping, thus supporting carbon sequestration strategies under a warming climate.

title: Exploring the coupling of ecosystem services and human well-being: evidence from Chinese cities through interpretable machine learning
abstract: • Multiple machine learning models to analyze the factors influencing. • The ESV-HDI coupling harmonization in China increased significantly. • Per capita forest area is the most important driving factor. • The driving factors exhibit nonlinear characteristics. • Climate change profoundly affects regional ecosystem services and human well-being. To achieve the development goal of harmonious coexistence within urban human–land systems, it is essential to conduct an in-depth exploration of the coupling coordination between human well-being and ecosystems. This study first constructs a human–land coupling system model to measure the coupling coordination degree between ecosystem service value and human well-being in Chinese cities. Second, box plots, kernel density analysis, and other methods are employed to investigate the spatiotemporal evolution characteristics of the coupling coordination degree. In addition, interpretable machine learning was applied to identify the feature importance, threshold effects, and interactions among variables affecting the coupling coordination degree. The results show that from 2000 to 2022, the coupling coordination degree between ESV and HDI in Chinese cities increased slowly, rising from 0.254 to 0.326. This improvement was mainly driven by the rapid growth of human well-being, with the HDI increasing from 0.526 to 0.784. The findings further confirm that both natural factors and human activities exert significant influences on the human–land coupling system, particularly variables such as per capita forest area, total land area, total population, per capita arable land, and precipitation. Moreover, the impact pathways of these variables exhibit nonlinear characteristics, with evident threshold effects. Precipitation, temperature, and sunshine duration show significant interaction effects with other variables. The findings contribute to monitoring the coordinated evolution of urban ecosystems and human well-being, and to promoting harmonious coexistence between humans and nature.

title: Identifying typical patterns of land-use and landscape structure in citizen science butterfly monitoring
abstract: • Cluster analysis reveals links between land use, landscape structure, and butterflies. • Butterfly diversity is highest in grassland- and forest-dominated landscapes. • Low-intensity grassland management seems most important in grassland-dominated landscapes. • Heterogenous landscape structure seems most important in crop-dominated landscapes. • Expanding German butterfly monitoring transects may enhance biodiversity assessments. Agricultural intensification in grasslands, characterized by increased livestock density, frequent mowing, and landscape homogenization, has driven significant declines in insect populations. Butterflies, key indicators of habitat quality, are sensitive to intensification and often used for monitoring. As they are influenced by the landscape context, understanding the landscapes surrounding monitoring transects is crucial for the evaluation of the status of butterflies and the effectiveness of conservation strategies. Using data from the German Butterfly Monitoring Scheme (DEBMS), we applied a nested clustering approach to group landscapes surrounding survey transects by dominant land cover, land-use intensity, and landscape structure. We then related these landscape contexts to butterfly diversity and community composition. Grassland- and forest-dominated clusters had highest species richness, abundance, number of specialists, and endangered species, while urban clusters had the lowest. Most species occurred independently of dominant land-cover types, highlighting the importance of even small proportions of habitats to support populations. We found no statistically significant differences in butterfly communities within crop- and grassland-dominated clusters when comparing different land-use intensity and landscape structure characteristics. However, data indicated higher richness, abundance, and more endangered species on less intensively managed grasslands. Our findings underscore the value of citizen science monitoring schemes in capturing broad-scale patterns in land use and landscape structure. Although clusters did not strongly differentiate distinct butterfly communities, they suggest that maintaining less intensively managed grasslands and expanding semi-natural habitats in agricultural landscapes can enhance butterfly diversity. We highlight the importance of accounting for landscape contexts when interpreting biodiversity patterns and informing conservation strategies.

title: Semi-natural habitats, red-listed plants and abandonment in Norway: patterns and a screening approach for prioritization
abstract: • 112,160 ha of farmland were continuously abandoned in Norway (2020–2024). • Only 3.7 % overlapped with mapped semi-natural ecosystems, mostly grasslands. • 3257 records of red-listed vascular plants found in abandoned semi-natural land. • 13.2 % of Norwegian municipalities showed significant NDVI greening trends over 7 years. • Mapping gaps and regional variation point to key areas for targeted management. Agricultural land abandonment is increasingly affecting rural and low-intensity farming regions across Europe, raising concerns about its impact on biodiversity. While some species may benefit from reduced human disturbance, many species in semi-natural ecosystem types depend on traditional agricultural management to maintain their ecological integrity. This study examines whether abandoned agricultural land in Norway contains semi-natural ecosystems that may hold important remnant populations of red-listed plant species and where continued cessation of farming may further threaten these biodiverse ecosystems. Using spatial data on abandoned farmland, semi-natural ecosystem types and species observations, we identify areas of conservation interest and assess the extent to which these areas support endangered species. In addition, we conducted a time-series analysis of vegetation change using NDVI data (2017–2024) to evaluate whether abandonment led to detectable ecological succession. We also analyzed the spatial distribution of abandonment and its correlation with proximity to active farms to understand regional patterns of abandonment. Our results show that only a small percentage (3.7 %) of the abandoned agricultural land considered in this study overlaps with known semi-natural ecosystem types, yet these areas support a significant number of red-listed plant species. The NDVI analysis revealed generally weak but positive greening trends, suggesting early successional changes that are not yet statistically significant across most habitat types. Our method thus suggests a potential approach to allocate limited management resources to key locations. At present, the amount of semi-natural ecosystems is probably underestimated, however, because of limited and time-consuming mapping activity. These findings emphasize the need for more extensive mapping and targeted conservation efforts and highlight the risks posed by abandonment in biodiversity rich semi-natural ecosystem types.

title: Corrigendum to “Integrating the AE-AM model and the SMI-P framework for water environmental security assessment: A case study of the Chushandian Reservoir basin”. [Ecol. Indic. 179 (2025) 114275]
Developing a carbon reduction potential indicator: a cross-level analysis of administrative regions in China based on a systematic review
Assessing post-harvest forest recovery using Landsat time series in temperate planted and natural forests
Integrating remote sensing and functional traits to elucidate estuarine common reed beds decline driven by soil salinity and anoxia
abstract: • Traits analysis and Sentinel 2 were used to study saltwater intrusion on reed beds. • Increasing salinity and anoxia reduced plant height and stem density in P.australis. • SLA remained unchanged, suggesting a conservative strategy under stress. • The IRECI index showed a strong relation with plant height. • Index trend analysis and image segmentation revealed habitat decline linked to marine influence. Reed beds play essential roles in wetland ecosystems, acting as natural filters and providing critical habitat for freshwater, estuarine, and marine species. However, increasing saltwater intrusion and soil anoxia caused by ongoing sea-level rise are affecting the integrity and functionality of these communities. This study aimed to assess the functional response of Phragmites australis (common reed) in a river delta in the North Adriatic Sea along a soil stress gradient assessing its functional trait variation and scaling these patterns via Sentinel-2 remote sensing in order to detect long-term ecosystem trends. Results showed that high soil salinity and anoxic conditions significantly reduced plant height and stem density, while leaf traits such as specific leaf area (SLA) remained unchanged, indicating a conservative adaptive strategy of the studied population. Plant height was able to clearly depict a plant growth trade-off under harsh environmental conditions showing solid positive relationships with the vegetation index used (Inverted Red-Edge Chlorophyll Index (IRECI), R 2 = 0.81), enabling the remote assessment of stress-induced changes. Satellite imagery analysis from 2017 to 2024 revealed an 11.3 % loss of reedbed cover, primarily in areas increasingly affected by marine influence. These findings suggested that rising sea levels and reduced freshwater inputs accelerated reedbed degradation in the Northern Adriatic Sea lagoons. The integration of functional ecology and remote sensing provided a powerful approach to monitoring wetland dynamics and assessing climate change impacts on coastal ecosystems.

title: Threshold effects of multi-scale landscape pattern on cultivated land ecosystem service in the Northeast Black Soil Region of China
abstract: • Trade-offs/synergies of Cultivated Land Ecosystem Services (CLESs) analyzed at county-level and grid scales. • Landscape-level metrics drive synergies at county-level scales, while patch-level metrics dominate at grid scales. • ENN_MN ≥ 0.464 and PAFRAC ≥ 0.941 boost FP and regulating service synergy. • Grassland > 18.1 % in cultivated land-dominated areas (>56.7 %) enhances multifunctionality. • Emphasizes scale-specific planning to balance agricultural productivity and ecology. Cultivated land systems play a dual role in food security and ecological sustainability, yet the mechanisms underlying trade-offs/synergies among ecosystem services remain unclear, particularly in intensively farmed regions. Focusing on the Northeast Black Soil Region (NBSR) of China, this study evaluated the trade-off/synergy relationships among Cultivated Land Ecosystem Services (CLESs) across multiple spatial scales, and identified threshold effects of landscape composition and configuration. We quantified five key services and applied Self-Organizing Maps (SOM) to classify service bundles. In addition, Random Forest (RF) and Multivariate Regression Tree (MRT) models were used to detect threshold effects of landscape patterns metrics on CLESs. The results reveal three findings: (1) interactions among CLESs are scale-dependent, with food production (FP) showing trade-offs with habitat quality (HQ) and carbon storage (CS) at the county scale, but shifting to synergies at the grid scale; (2) at the county scale, service synergies are primarily driven by landscape-level metrics, such as connectivity and diversity, whereas grid scale synergies depend on patch-level metrics like habitat composition (e.g., grassland, woodland and cultivated land) and their shape complexity; (3) distinct threshold effects were identified, e.g., high landscape connectivity (ENN_MN ≥ 0.464) and boundary complexity (PAFRAC ≥ 0.941) jointly enhance functional complementarity between FP and regulating services such as water yield (WY) and carbon storage (CS). Conversely, increasing grassland proportion (PLAND_GL > 18.1 %) in cultivated land-dominated areas (PLAND_CUL > 56.7 %) significantly strengthens ecosystem service coordination. These findings highlight the necessity of scale-specific, spatially explicit strategies to enhance both agricultural productivity and ecological resilience, offering actionable guidance for sustainable black soil management.

title: Dominant hydrological drivers of vegetation pattern changes in a river-connected lake after dam construction: outlet or inlet?
abstract: • The water–sediment environment of Dongting Lake was significantly altered by Three Gorges Dam. • Inundation patterns affected wetland vegetation distribution and succession. • Reduced water depth resulted in the space encroachment of Reed on Carex after Three Gorges Dam construction. • Water level change at the outlet was the major contributor to vegetation succession. Understanding the relationships between the spatiotemporal characteristics of vegetation and key hydrological factors is crucial for maintaining ecosystem stability in river-connected lakes. However, the complex hydrological interactions between the inlets and outlets of these lakes and rivers influence the direction and rate of vegetation succession, making wetland vegetation restoration in river-connected lakes more challenging. This study focused on Dongting Lake, an example of a river-connected lake in China, and examined the spatiotemporal variations in inundation and vegetation patterns following the construction of the Three Gorges Dam (TGD). Using the hydrodynamic model MIKE 21, we evaluated the contribution of hydrological conditions at the outlet and inlet to vegetation changes. The results revealed that after TGD operation, water discharge from the three channels and the water level at the outlet dramatically reduced, leading to a decrease in inundation duration and depth, particularly in East Dongting Lake. Concurrently, the vegetation area expanded and moved toward the lake’s center. The suitable inundation durations for Carex and Reed were 132–240 d and 110–186 d, respectively, suggesting that reduced water depths favored Reed growth and exacerbated the encroachment of Reed on Carex . Additionally, the decline in the water level at the outlet was identified as the key factor influencing vegetation succession in Dongting Lake after the TGD began operation. Therefore, water level regulation is key to mitigating the adverse impacts of the TGD on the lake’s ecosystem. This work provides significant insights for the restoration of wetland vegetation in river-connected lakes impacted by dams.

title: A new perspective on estimating Chlorophyll-a concentrations using machine learning and remote sensing: a case study of New York state lakes
abstract: Algal bloom proliferation across the United States has been increasing in congruence with several anthropogenically influenced processes. Challenges in monitoring algal bloom growth include the high labor and equipment requirements necessary to quantify algal presence which makes widespread availability of data limited. In New York, USA, where numerous inland lakes experience severe anthropogenic impacts, only a fraction of the over 7,000 lakes have reliable quantitative algal bloom data. Operational remote sensing can be used to fill the gap in unmonitored lakes, though previous techniques do not accommodate small lakes due to spatial resolution capabilities, atmospheric correction algorithms, and lack of a comprehensive empirical formula. In this study, we used Landsat-8 and -9, (2013-2023), and Sentinel-2 (2019-2023), processed with inland water-based atmospheric correction techniques, and joined geospatial watershed characteristics to model algal presence in New York lakes. We implemented several machine learning models and found Extra Trees Regression to be the best performing with marginal error (R2 = 0.72, RMSE = 8.19 mg/l). From these results, we can obtain a comprehensive view of algal blooms across New York from 2013 - the present, which can inform stakeholders of the trends in presence and concentrations in both large and small lakes. Results from this study will be made available on a public interface that will contain in situ data, key lake characteristics, model time-series, and model raster predictions. This model procedure is easily replicable for expansion outside of New York State and can be expanded to include more lakes in other regions.

title: County-scale assessment of Spartina alterniflora spread risk in Hebei’s coastal areas using the MaxEnt model
abstract: • County-scale risk mapping supports targeted local control and management policies. • Multisource remote sensing images identified Spartina alterniflora current distribution. • Temperature-related variables are key drivers of S. alterniflora invasion risk. • Cross-county invasion risk emphasizes the need for joint regional control strategies. Spartina alterniflora spread and invasion risks have been extensively studied at global and national scales in recent years, there remains a lack of targeted guidance for control policies and measures at the county level, where practical implementation typically occurs. This study identified the current distribution of Spartina alterniflora using multi-source data from various remote sensing images and predicted its spread and invasion risks across the coastal counties of Hebei Province using the Maxent model. The results showed that: (1) Huanghua and Fengnan counties are the core distribution areas of Spartina alterniflora in Hebei Province. Specially, Huanghua County contains 7% high-risk and 32% medium-risk areas, while Fengnan County includes 29% and 37%, respectively; (2) The most important variables in this study as follows in order: average diurnal temperature range in June, exchangeable sodium salt of the top sediment, average diurnal ground temperature range in June, accumulated temperature from March to June, elevation; (3) Huanghua and Fengnan counties should be prioritized for Spartina alterniflora control, while continuous monitoring remain essential in the middle intertidal zone of other counties, and micro-topographic modification is advocated in high- and medium-risk areas to change its environmental suitability. Finally, this study highlights the importance of incorporating tidal level and hydrodynamic conditions in future research.

title: Evaluation of water quality characteristics, spatiotemporal variations, and pollution sources apportionment in the Beijing-Hangzhou Grand Canal, Eastern China
abstract: • DO, COD Mn , COD, BOD 5 , NH 3 -N, and TP were comprehensively evaluated across the Beijing-Hangzhou Grand Canal. • The modified Water Quality Index (WQI-DET) reflected the spatiotemporal dynamics of water quality along the Grand Canal. • Study identified the critical variables causing water quality deterioration at 20 monitoring sites. • SHAP interpretation combined with RFR model was applied to identify the primary driving factors influencing water quality. Effective management of large urban rivers requires accurately identifying the spatiotemporal drivers of key indicator exceedances and apportioning pollution sources from the latest monitoring data, thereby providing actionable insights for watershed administrators. The Beijing-Hangzhou Grand Canal, as the world’s longest artificial river and a vital “golden waterway” traversing several central cities in eastern China, plays an essential role in regional development. This study systematically evaluated its water quality patterns and spatiotemporal dynamics using a novel Water Quality Index (WQI-DET), which can better reflect water quality conditions and identify the causes of water quality deterioration, incorporating six key indicators: dissolved oxygen (DO), permanganate index (COD Mn ), chemical oxygen demand (COD), biochemical oxygen demand (BOD 5 ), ammonia nitrogen (NH 3 -N), and the total phosphorus (TP). Our analysis uncovered marked spatial and seasonal fluctuations, with water quality deteriorating notably during summer. The WQI-DET values also revealed that key indicators influencing water quality deterioration exhibited distinct seasonal and spatial variability. DO emerged as the dominant deterioration factor in summer, while TP played the leading role in other seasons. Spatially, COD Mn -related pollution was more severe in the northern section of the canal, whereas NH 3 -N contamination predominated in the southern reaches. This study adopted Random Forest Regression (RFR) coupled with SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) method to identify the primary drivers of water quality dynamics. To facilitate effective and actionable watershed management, this study considered various variables (30 in total), including environmental, socioeconomical, and industrial structure factors. The results highlighted that irrigated area, fertilizer application, temperature, precipitation, and livestock rearing (pigs and sheep) were the dominant contributors to exceedance across all six indicators. These findings enhance comprehension of the mechanisms underlying water quality variation along the Grand Canal, offering valuable insights for targeted and effective regional water quality management.

title: Evapotranspiration components and its driving mechanism in a sandy shrubland
abstract: Accurate characterization of evapotranspiration (ET) and its components in sandy shrublands and understanding its driving mechanisms are essential for desertification control and water management in desert regions. However, considerable limitations remain regarding the estimation accuracy of ET and its components in sandy shrubland, as well as the driving mechanism of the proportion of each component. Using long-term (2015–2022) in situ observations from a typical Caragana microphylla shrubland in the Horqin Sandy Land of China, this study improved canopy surface resistance and soil surface resistance in the original dual-source ET model and integrated random simulation algorithm to optimize empirical parameters. The improved model significantly outperformed the original dual-source model, with the R2value increasing by 20% and RMSE and MAE decreasing by 55% and 31%, respectively. During the growing seasons from 2015 to 2022, ET ranged from 0.02 to 6.38 mm/d with the average of 1.73 mm/d at daily timescale, and the dynamic of ET was primarily driven by the precipitation and vegetation conditions. The annual ratio of ET to precipitation (P) ET/P ranged from 0.71 to 0.83, with ET being the primary component in precipitation allocation. The T/ET varied between 0.22 and 0.67 at monthly timescale, peaking during the vigorous growth stage compared to the early and late growing stages, primarily controlled by the Leaf Area Index (LAI), and its influence on T/ET became more pronounced when LAI exceeded 1.6. The Caragana microphylla community exhibited a water surplus, with the difference between annual P and ET (P-ET) ranging from 80.77 to 142.07 mm, and it was mainly governed by precipitation characteristics. ET dominated the water balance, and played a more significant role during drought period. This study indicated that water and vegetation conditions jointly regulated the distribution process of P and ET, which was of great significance for water management and ecological restoration in desertification regions.

title: Contrasting responses of Norway spruce (Picea abies (L.) H.Karst) and European beech (Fagus sylvatica L.) seedlings to warming in the Western Carpathians: growth, root and leaf traits, physiology
abstract: • Soil warming affected spruce and beech seedlings differently. • Spruce showed reduced growth, slight pigment loss and impaired photochemistry. • Beech exhibited enhanced growth and stable physiological performance. • Leaf and needle shape traits responded strongly to warming. • Warming may shift seedling competition and forest regeneration patterns. Climate warming is expected to influence forest regeneration, particularly in mountain ecosystems. However, experimental evidence on how key European tree species respond to warming during the early stages of development remains limited. We conducted an in-situ experiment to assess the impact of warming on year-old seedling performance of Norway spruce ( Picea abies (L.) H.Karst.) and European beech ( Fagus sylvatica L.) in the Western Carpathians. One-year-old seedlings were grown for nearly 500 days under ambient and warmed conditions using open top chambers, which increased mean topsoil temperature by 0.25 °C on average. In total, 160 seedlings were assessed through comprehensive biometric and physiological analyses. Our results revealed contrasting species-specific responses. Spruce seedlings exhibited significantly reduced height (by 23 %) and root biomass (by 52 %) under warming, while beech maintained or slightly increased growth. Biomass allocation patterns also diverged: spruce allocated less to roots under warming, while beech remained stable. Warming caused beech leaves to become longer and wider, while spruce needles became shorter and narrower – patterns were derived from measurements of over 30,000 spruce needles and 2,300 beech leaves. Physiological assessments showed a slight decrease in chlorophyll content and reduced efficiency of the light phase of photosynthesis in spruce, while beech displayed stable pigment concentrations and photochemical performance. These findings highlight the vulnerability of cold-adapted spruce and the adaptive plasticity of more thermophilic beech under warming, suggesting potential shifts in competitive dynamics and forest composition, with implications for future management strategies.

title: Assessing thermal comfort in a landmark urban park: a case study and methodological framework of Alamo Square in San Francisco, USA
abstract: • A framework combining social media data and microclimate data predicted activity. • Microclimate factors prove more impactful than facility factors. • Post-reforestation vegetation reduced hot stress but increased cold stress. • Post-reforestation shaded zones often mismatched activity hubs. Urban green spaces are increasingly challenged by climate stressors, yet strategies for climate-adaptive renewal are often difficult to evaluate in culturally and historically significant sites. This study exames Alamo Square in San Francisco, a globally recognized tourist landmark parkas a single-case analysis of how incremental reforestation and shading interventions influence human activity patterns and thermal comfort. This study integrates geotagged social media data (Flickr/Instagram), ENVI-met microclimate simulations, and spatial statistical analyses (Kernel Density Estimation, hot spot analysis). Focusing on Alamo Square’s reforestation initiativeaimed at doubling tree density with drought-tolerant species-the research reveals that pre-intervention activity clustered densely near the iconic “Painted Ladies,” driven by tourism. Post-reforestation, vegetation significantly reduced summer PET values, dispersing heat stress zones, but introduced winter cold zones and spatial mismatches between shaded areas and emergent activity hubs. Rest facilities (e.g., shaded seating) consistently outperformed entertainment amenities in attracting users, highlighting their role in thermal adaptation. This work innovatively combines dynamic crowdsourced data with human-centered thermal metrics to expose seasonal trade-offs, advocating for designs that align cooling interventions with activity hot spots while mitigating winter discomfort. The findings demonstrate that effective urban green space design requires balancing ecological goals (e.g., canopy restoration) with human-centered strategies, such as strategic shading of high-traffic paths. By bridging environmental modeling and behavioral analytics, this study offers transferable insights and practical ecological indicators for landmark or tourism-driven parks to evaluate thermal comfort and enhance preparedness for future climatic challenges.

title: First-time application of the IUCN urban Nature Indexes and its applicability for urban-related biodiversity conservation targets – A case study for Berlin, Germany
abstract: • First-time application of the Urban Nature Indexes (UNI) − for Berlin city in 2023. • UNI can support cities in assessing and achieving biodiversity targets. • UNI indicators cover all urban targets of biodiversity frameworks. • The application of UNI depends on the city’s data availability. • Scientific and political measures are needed for effective UNI implementation. Urbanisation is increasing rapidly worldwide and is one of the major pressures on the environment and its biodiversity. Therefore, biodiversity change in urban areas is considered an issue in several global, EU and regional biodiversity conservation frameworks. In order to meet urban-related targets, the status of urban biodiversity must first be assessed to provide a baseline for future evaluations. Cities are not only drivers of change and transformation, they are also the places where decisions will be made about how we will live on this planet in the future. In 2022, the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) developed the Urban Nature Indexes (UNI) to measure the ecological performance of cities and evaluate the effectiveness of conservation initiatives in urban ecosystems. The UNI consists of six themes and 30 indicators, covering a multidimensional approach to measuring urban ecological impacts. This study presents the first-time application of the UNI, realised in 2023 for the German capital Berlin, demonstrating the data sources used for 27 indicators and providing an example for other cities interested in applying the UNI. Furthermore, we demonstrate that all UNI indicators cover urban-related targets and areas of action of global, EU, and regional biodiversity frameworks. The UNI have the potential to support cities in achieving and evaluating targets implemented through policy for urban biodiversity conservation, which could play an important role in addressing the global biodiversity crisis.

title: Miankaleh International Wetland: toxic element hazards and possibility of botulinum poisoning
abstract: Miankaleh Wetland, located in the southeast of the Caspian Sea, is a rich ecosystem and an international haven for wintering of migratory waterbirds in Asia. Moreover, it is the most important caviar producing area in Iran. This wetland has attracted great attention due to the death of thousands of birds and fish related to Clostridium botulinum poisoning in recent years. Considering the limited previous studies in Miankaleh Wetland, which were confined to sampling sediment in a limited number of stations and continuous input of pollutants, further research on sediments and water of this wetland is essential. So, this study aimed to evaluate the physicochemical features of water and sediments as a key indicator in botulinum poisoning, occurrence of potentially toxic elements (PTE), sources and environmental hazards. For this purpose, 95 and 40 site selected for sampling of sediment and water, respectively. Results showed that most of water samples exhibit low dissolved oxygen, low redox potential, and relatively high pH and electrical conductivity (EC) with mean 7.82 mg/l, 63.69 mV, 8.3, 15.10 mS/Cm, respectively. Also, sediment samples contain high organic matter and high EC, with mean 9.01 % and 13.29 mS/Cm, respectively. So, botulinum contamination is a possibility based on the physicochemical properties of water and sediments. Maximum concentrations of some PTE in Miankaleh water exceed the corresponding safety thresholds. And also, the maximum concentrations of all PTE in the sediment samples exceed the background and Caspian Sea sediment value. Based on SOM, PMF analyses, and sequential extraction results there are three major contributors of PTE in Miankaleh Wetland. But PTE contamination does not appear to be a likely factor in birds and fishes poisoning. However, to prevent future disasters, it is crucial to manage wastewater entering Miankaleh Wetland to preserve the physicochemical properties of the water and sediment.

title: Environmental RNA as a transformative tool for aquatic ecosystem health assessment: progress and challenges
abstract: • The feasibility exploration of eRNA technology is summarized. • General workflow of eRNA technology is proposed. • Applications of eRNA is wide and has a great potential. • Point out the “mists” of eRNA technology. The assessment of aquatic ecosystem health is undergoing a paradigm shift from traditional physicochemical monitoring to molecular biological monitoring. As an innovative biomonitoring tool, environmental RNA (eRNA) offers advantages such as a short persistence time and correlation with metabolic gene expression, which effectively reduce false-positive detection rates and identify metabolically active communities, providing real-time information on biological assemblages. Compared to environmental DNA (eDNA), eRNA possesses unique diagnostic capabilities for assessing living organisms and their functional states. The use of eRNA technology to obtain real-time transcriptional information can provide physiological insights into species. When combined with eDNA technology, it can achieve a relatively ideal effect while saving human and material resources compared to traditional techniques. Nevertheless, eRNA technology still faces challenges related to feasibility verification, improvement and optimization of detection methods, construction of application frameworks, and promotion of field experiments. Despite its promise, eRNA technology remains in its infancy and lacks comprehensive reviews synthesizing current research progress. To address this gap, we present a systematic analysis of eRNA studies to examine the technical characteristics and practical feasibility of this approach. We further outline standardized eRNA workflows and highlight its diverse applications, including (1) biodiversity monitoring, (2) physiological status assessment, (3) immune response evaluation and pathogen detection, and (4) assessment of environmental stress responses. We also identify unresolved questions (“mists”) around theory, methodology, and application. Finally, we discuss the impacts of these “mists” and propose possible solutions and future research directions. The potential of eRNA extends beyond species detection, revolutionizing aquatic ecosystem health monitoring by facilitating the acquisition of multidimensional biological data. In the future, eRNA technology is expected to be applied across diverse fields, including conservation biology, ecotoxicology, environmental health science, and ecosystem management. However, many obstacles must be overcome before it can be widely adopted in practical applications.

title: The feedback mechanism between water culture and water security in the Yellow River Basin
abstract: • Quantitative expression of the evolution of water culture. • A framework for the co-evolution of water culture and water security is constructed. • Explained the mutual feedback mechanism of water culture and water security. In the context of escalating global water resource challenges, examining the response of water cultural changes to water security and their governance becomes imperative for sustainable water management. Water culture can be seen as a reflection of how human values orient towards the utilization and safeguarding of water resources. However, in the current governance of water security, greater attention needs to be paid to water culture. By analyzing how the three subsystems of water security (i.e., water disaster, water resources, and water ecology) and external factors influence the evolution and behavioral response of water culture, this study explores the mutual feedback relationship between water culture and water security in the Yellow River Basin. It also establishes a conceptual coupling model of water culture and water security, and reveals the process through which water culture transforms from meeting water resource exploitation needs to prioritizing ecological protection. This research promotes the adjustment and optimization of the governance mechanisms for water security. By gaining a deeper understanding of the far-reaching impacts of evolving water culture on water security, policymakers can develop more adaptive and resilient policies to effectively address increasingly complex water security challenges.

title: Water provisioning services under changing land use and climate scenarios in the lower Shivaliks of Uttarakhand, India
abstract: • Water yield increased on the spatial–temporal scale due to the expansion of impervious surfaces and associated runoff. • Precipitation, population density, and maximum temperature were attributable for water provision service. • Climate had stronger influence than land use on water yield. Dehradun Forest Division (covering 861.48 sq km of geographical area) of lower Himalayas, India contribute to people in variety of ways including water provision, constituted by Asan and Song watersheds and is facing climatic and anthropogenic challenges. Present study aims to quantitatively assess water provision service under changing land use and climate scenarios. Land use and land cover map was made using Landsat data for 1995, 2005, 2015 and 2022. Forest was the dominant class (more than ∼ 70 % of the geographical area) with increasing built-up area (4.85 %) and a reduction of forest (4.30 %) between 1995–2022. InVEST (Annual Water Yield) model was used to estimate water yield (WY) at spatial–temporal scale. Geographical Detector Modelling was applied to identify the potential factors influencing the distribution of water provision. The overall volume of WY increased from 1995 to 2015 with a slight decrease in 2022 with Song has more water provision than the Asan at watershed scale. Bare ground (28.02 %) and built-up (26.54 %) had highest WY due to impact of surface runoff pertaining to impervious soil structure with minimal infiltration belowground. Water provision service were found to be mainly impacted by precipitation, population density, and maximum temperature. Scenario based analysis further substantiated that changes in climate and land use strongly impacted water retention by forest in differential manner. Based on spatial scale and landscape composition of the watersheds, 97.21 % of the area was under trade-off with other nature’s contribution to people. The study provides results that highlight the spatial and temporal dynamics in water yield across various land use classes and forest types, emphasizing on the importance of forest ecosystem in lower Himalayas and their significant contribution to people. This study provides information on water security of urbanizing watersheds in Himalayan ecosystem based on scientific basis and assist policymakers to design resilient forest conservation frameworks, ensuring the long-term ecological stability.

title: Assessing the steppe vulnerability to extreme climate events in the Inner Mongolia
abstract: • The vulnerability assessment model was constructed by Expose-Sensitivity-Resilience. • A 17-year moving window method was used to analyze the time characteristics of vulnerability elements. • The trend changes in exposure and sensitivity play a dominant role in the trend changes of vulnerability. • High temperature events have a significant negative impact on Steppe VI. Global warming has intensified extreme weather events, leading to significant changes in vegetation dynamics and highlighting the urgent need for a systematic assessment of ecosystem vulnerability. As a typical ecologically fragile region in northern China, the Inner Mongolian grasslands represent a critical area for such research. To assess the vulnerability of vegetation ecosystems in Inner Mongolia to climate change, we conducted a comprehensive evaluation by integrating exposure, sensitivity, and resilience in parallel. We computed 17 extreme climate indices for the Inner Mongolia. We applied Theil-Sen trend analysis, the Mann-Kendall test, and geographic detector models to characterize the spatiotemporal dynamics and driving factors of grassland vulnerability to extreme climate events in Inner Mongolia. The results indicated that from 1982 to 2018, extreme climatic events in Inner Mongolia exhibited a decline in precipitation coupled with an increase in temperature, while Gross Primary Production (GPP) demonstrated a statistically insignificant increased trend (0.003 gC·m −2 ·a −1 ).Spatially, extreme precipitation events exhibited an increased trend in the western regions and a decreased trend in the eastern regions, while a general intensification of high-temperature events was observed across Inner Mongolia. The spatial distribution of GPP changes reveals an increase in the southern regions and a decrease in the northern regions. Exposure and sensitivity are the dominant factors driving vulnerability changes in the grassland ecosystems of Inner Mongolia, with extreme heat events playing a critical role in exacerbating vulnerability, particularly in desert steppes.

title: Succession-driven dynamics of ecosystem function and multifunctionality at regional scales: Evidence from subtropical secondary forests
Machine learning-based assessment of grassland degradation levels on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau from 2000 to 2020
abstract: • A novel remote sensing framework assessed grassland degradation. • Combining eco-geographical zones and space-for-time substitution method. • Degradation intensified from east to west with 13.4 % recovered and 8.7 % remained degraded. • Human activity and climate interactions dominated degradation drivers. Remote sensing (RS) technology is an indispensable tool for grassland degradation monitoring and assessment at the regional scale. However, most of these remote sensing-based grassland degradation applications rely on a limited set of common indicators (e.g., fractional vegetation coverage (FVC), net primary productivity (NPP) or aboveground biomass) that are monitored through time series, which makes these methods not comprehensive and explicit enough for direct spatial comparison. In this study, we developed a remote sensing monitoring framework for grassland degradation that integrates eco-geographical zones with a space-for-time substitution approach on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau (QTP). Five grassland eco-geographical zones were established based on long term abiotic (climatic and geographic) and biotic (NPP) data to ensure consistent degradation assessment criteria under similar environmental conditions and comparable grassland states. By integrating field data of grassland degradation level and regional indicators (FVC, NPP as well as soil conservation (SC) and water retention (WR)), also considering the spatial heterogeneity of grasslands across different eco-geographical zones, we assessed grassland degradation on the QTP with overall accuracy reaching 0.87. We detected high spatial heterogeneity in grassland degradation levels across the QTP, with a trend of increasing severity from east to west. The average area of no, slight, moderate and heavy degradation accounted for 33.4 %, 25.3 %, 14.8 %, and 26.6 % of the total grassland area on the QTP in the 2000–2020 period. Temporal dynamics analysis revealed that 13.4 % of grassland showed recovery trends, while 8.7 % maintained stable degradation status, with the remainder demonstrating either no significant change or dynamic equilibrium. Furthermore, the key drivers influencing the spatial distribution of grassland degradation were investigated with a geographical detector model. The human activity intensity index (HAI) exhibited the highest explanatory power among individual factors (q = 0.75). Notably, the interaction between mean annual precipitation and degree-days below 18 °C (q = 0.98) emerged as the dominant factor, emphasizing the strong interaction influence of climatic variables in shaping grassland degradation patterns across the QTP. Our study introduces a method for assessing grassland degradation level considering spatial variation of grassland, which provides more explicit information for management and sustainable development of grassland ecosystems compared with traditional methods.

title: Dung beetle communities are jointly mediated by soil properties, herbivore dung types, and habitats in Serengeti savannah
abstract: • Dung beetle communities vary significantly across Serengeti habitats. • Generalist dung use observed with minimal herbivore dung specialization. • Soil properties, habitats and dung types jointly shape dung beetle structure. • Random Forest and SEM reveals key predictors and their causal-effect relationships. • Results highlights dung beetles as bioindicators of savannah ecosystems. Dung beetles play essential roles in ecosystem functioning, by decomposing mammalian dungs, thereby facilitate nutrient cycling, seed dispersal, and parasite suppression. However, dung beetle communities and their driving factors in the Serengeti savannah remains poorly investigated. We investigated spatial patterns in dung beetle abundance, diversity, and community composition and their driving factors, using pitfall traps baited with wildebeest, buffalo, and zebra dungs along established transects spanning three habitat types: grassland, wooded grassland, and bushland. Our results demonstrated significant variation in the dung beetle assemblages among-habitat types. Specifically, open grasslands exhibited higher species richness and diversity, along with distinct compositional shifts. Dung preference analysis revealed a generalist pattern in resource use, with limited specialization to herbivore dung types. The Random Forest model explained 33%, 50%, and 52% of variance in abundance, diversity, and species richness respectively, with the key predictors being habitats, vegetation cover, herbivore dung type, and soil characteristics including electrical conductivity, soil texture, moisture, and temperature. Structural equation model further indicated that: 1) species richness was directly influenced by dung types, habitats, and vegetation cover; 2) abundance was affected by soil moisture; and 3) community composition was shaped by temperature. These findings demonstrate dung beetle communities are jointly regulated by soil properties, vegetation structure, habitat characteristics, and dung resources; key factors that maintain beetle populations and potentially enhance ecosystem multifunctionality. As bioindicators, dung beetle species provide the critical insights for biodiversity conservation. We recommend prioritizing the conservation of diverse herbivores and heterogeneous habitats to ensure resource continuity for dung beetles in Serengeti and analogous ecosystems.

title: Lake trophic state indicator shows non-stationary relationships with environmental drivers
abstract: Understanding drivers of water quality is critical for anticipating and managing lake ecosystems under global change. While theoretical relationships between drivers (air temperature) and water quality (chlorophyll-a) are well understood, it remains unclear whether these relationships remain stationary. Further, the temporal scale over which data are analyzed may influence driver-response relationships. To identify changing relationships, we fit univariate autoregressive models between drivers and lake trophic state over 20+ years in Lake Rotoehu, New Zealand using the Trophic Level Index (TLI), a widely used ecological indicator of lake water quality and nutrient status. We tested model performance over three window types: 1) the full time series, 2) three discrete 8-year windows, and 3) 8-year moving windows. Model performance and significance varied over time, indicating non-stationarity between drivers and TLI. Additionally, driver importance to the TLI also varied over window type. Specifically, meteorological and internal loading drivers were top predictors during full and discrete windows, but moving windows revealed the importance of other drivers (e.g., water level) which would otherwise have been unidentified. Examination of model parameters revealed that direction and magnitude of driver-TLI relationships also varied over window type, indicating that parameter values fit over a single window may not capture variability in relationships. We demonstrate the importance of using trophic state indicators dynamically, acknowledging shifting driver-response relationships to support adaptive freshwater management under environmental change.

title: Navigating the complexity of coastal seas: Poor representation of taxonomic and functional benthic communities by abiotic habitat classifications
abstract: • Abiotic habitat maps poorly reflect benthic communities in the Dutch Wadden Sea. • Biotic clustering enhances marine conservation and management decisions. • Trait-based methods support scalable and standardised habitat mapping. • Functional traits provide strong indicators for ecosystem-based spatial planning. • Large-scale biotic monitoring is key to effective spatial planning. Ecosystem-based Marine Spatial Planning (MSP) requires good habitat mapping to balance socioeconomic and ecological interests. Habitat types with similar abiotic conditions, or physiotopes, are commonly used as proxies for ecological communities due to the availability of high-resolution environmental data. However, similar physiotopes may host different ecological communities, for example, due to strong species-environment feedback or priority effects. Moreover, mapping ecological functions through biological traits offers further insights into ecosystem services and vulnerability to human impacts, improving ecosystem-based MSP. Using the Dutch Wadden Sea as a case study, we classified macrozoobenthic communities (biotopes) at taxonomic and functional levels, assessing how well current physiotopes represent these communities. We used spatially explicit monitoring data from 5314 stations and applied hierarchical clustering with adaptive branch tuning to identify communities. A Random Forest model was then trained to predict their distribution from environmental gradients. We identified 14 taxonomic and 10 functional communities, often occurring across multiple physiotopes. Existing physiotopes poorly predicted biological community structure, explaining only 14 % of taxonomic and 9 % of functional variation. In contrast, biotopes explained 46 % (taxonomic) and 66 % (functional) variation, showing stronger ecological relevance. Each biotope was associated with distinct species or traits, aiding identification of sensitive communities. Our findings show that physiotope boundaries currently used in spatial planning do not reflect biological realities and fail to capture ecologically significant areas. Our findings highlight the need for an integrated approach combining biotic and abiotic mapping to optimise ecosystem-based MSP to facilitate more specific protection of sensitive and functionally important communities.

title: Corrigendum to “Leveraging local wildlife surveys for robust occupancy trend estimation”. [Ecol. Indic. 169 (2024) 112863]
Corrigendum to “Identification of spatial pathways for aquatic ecological risk spread under multi-stressor synergies: A case study of the Pinglu Canal” [Ecol. Indic. 178 (2025) 113915]
Assessment and early warning of the coupled carrying capacity of water resources, environment, and ecology: A case study of Ordos
abstract: Water resources, water environment, and water ecology are interrelated and mutually influential, playing a critical role in integrated water system planning and high-quality economic development. Three-dimensional water system (water resources, environment, and ecology) carrying capacity (TDWCC) is crucial to regional development and sustainable growth. This study established a Driving–Pressure–State–Impact–Response (DPSIR) model and coupled it with the deal solution similarity ranking technique (TOPSIS) to evaluate the TDWCC in Ordos. By integrating entropy weight with variable weight, the comprehensive indicator weights are determined for assessing TDWCC. Based on TDWCC status and potential future trends, the risk of TDWCC in 2030, 2040, and 2050 is predicted. The results indicate that the overall TDWCC in Ordos increased from 0.35 in 2000 to 0.59 in 2023 indicating a slightly weak carrying capacity. Kangbashi District saw rapid improvement due to better infrastructure and water management policies. From 2016 to 2023, its TDWCC grade increased from Grade III to Grade IV. In contrast, Jungar Banner consistently remained at Grade II or Grade III due to limited water resources and high industrial water consumption. Among the five subsystems, the pressure and impact subsystems exhibit relatively high carrying capacity. In 2030, TDWCC temporarily declines to 0.51, elevating the warning level to serious warning. In 2040 and 2050, it is projected to rise to 0.63 and 0.68 respectively, entering the mild warning range. The key driver of TDWCC in Ordos is ecological flow satisfaction, green area coverage and water use per unit of industrial value added (in RMB 10,000). In the future, efforts to enhance regional water resource carrying capacity should focus on optimizing the spatial allocation of water resources, adjusting water use structures, improving ecological regulation capacity, and strengthening the water governance system. The findings of this study provide decision-making support for the sustainable utilization and zoned management of water resources in Ordos, and offer theoretical guidance for water ecological governance in resource-constrained cities.

title: Protected area management effectiveness is pivotal in nature-based solutions for carbon neutrality: A tale from the Eastern Arc Mountains, Tanzania
The effects of stream hydromorphology on fish communities in the central European Alps
abstract: Many freshwater fish species rely on specific hydrological and morphological stream characteristics and are sensitive to their changes. However, the incomplete understanding of hydromorphological processes responsible for changes and their effect on fish populations creates further difficulties in conserving and managing these ecosystems. In this study, we analysed the effects of river hydromorphology on fish communities by using the recently introduced Hydromorphology Index (IHM). The IHM was developed based on European standards in a study area composed of 80 representative stream sections in a transect of conditions from nearly natural to highly anthropogenically influenced in the Alps of Italy and Austria. The IHM is a combination of the hydrological index (based on three indicators) and the morphological index (a set of eight indicators). Fish diversity, abundance, and biomass were highly correlated with riverbed and riverbank vegetation. The IHM provided strong evidence for understanding fish communities and thus, gives more information about stream conditions. This study shows that the IHM provides a standardised methodology to collect data on historical and future changes in river morphology and hydrology in a uniform manner and subsequently relates these to changes in the fish fauna. The results of this study establish an important foundation in the form of a summarising index to enable decision-makers to prioritise measures for improving fish habitats.

title: Generic ‘nature-based’ framing may distort understanding of the effectiveness of hydrometeorological risk reduction measures
abstract: The use of natural features for hydrometeorological risk reduction has been recently promoted in international strategies and led to an increasing number of actions framed, in particular, as nature-based solutions (NbS). This has sparked a growing debate about the performative role of these concepts in shaping the funding landscape. While several frameworks have been proposed to evaluate the NbS implementation, they can only be effectively applied if NbS and evaluation indicators are clearly defined within and across the individual projects. In this article, we draw upon knowledge representation theory and we provide an evolutionary analysis of the NbS and related concepts and a review of current funding calls in Europe (n = 53) and individual projects globally (n = 342). This allows us to show how NbS have become dominant in recent practical discussions on hydrometeorological risk reduction. While terminological framing as NbS is needed to link individual projects to pre-existing knowledge, our analysis reveals that it can also tend to leverage and legitimise funding. This leads to adverse effects on expert knowledge-building especially in urban settings where hydrometeorological risk reduction necessitates complex approaches, integrating various measures. We assert that too generic NbS framing introduces additional uncertainty in assessments of NbS effectiveness and potentially excludes other viable measures from consideration and implementation. We therefore argue that coherence between the stated NbS and the indicators capturing effectiveness of actual set of measures is critical for gaining evidence from monitoring of hydrometeorological risk reduction projects. For these purposes, we propose a guideline for transparent reporting of aims, concepts, implementation outcomes, and indicators for projects aiming at hydrometeorological risk reduction. Our work highlights the need for global coherence, cross-sectoral knowledge integration, and context-sensitive evaluations to ensure that NbS deliver multiple co-benefits beyond risk reduction.

title: Remarkable conservation effects for Amazon protected areas in vegetation growth trend, stability, and vulnerability
abstract: • Amazon PAs were comprehensively evaluated by trend, stability, and vulnerability. • PAs exerted remarkable conservation effects on Amazon vegetation since 2000. • Vegetation growth enhanced yet stability reduced and vulnerability increased. • Vegetation declined while conservation improved across SP, NSP, and IP PAs. Protected Areas (PAs) have been widely recognized as a crucial strategy to conserve biodiversity and maintain ecosystem services and functions, especially for the Amazon basin, the world’s largest tropical rainforest. Assessing the conservation effectiveness of Amazonian PAs is therefore imperative, given intensifying disturbances observed in the Amazon basin. However, current studies typically focus solely on vegetation growth trend while neglecting ecological vulnerability and ecosystem stability, potentially leading to biased conclusions. Here, we evaluated the conservation effectiveness of Amazon PAs since 2000 by introducing a comprehensive Composite Indicator (CI) that integrates vegetation growth trend, stability, and vulnerability dimensions into consideration. Results indicate that 87 % of the analyzed pixels within Amazon PAs exhibited greening trends since 2000, while browning trends were primarily concentrated in the northwestern Amazon PAs. A ‘green paradox’ was observed across the Amazon PAs, where the higher vegetation growth trends were associated with increased vulnerability and decreased stability, highlighting the necessity of incorporating vulnerability and stability when assessing conservation effectiveness of PAs. We reported the conservation effectiveness in Amazon PAs since 2000 to be significant, with vegetation status as indicated by the CI metric being higher inside than outside PAs in 72 % of Amazon PAs. PAs with better vegetation status outside than inside were distributed along a southwestern-to-northeastern transect of the Amazon basin. Notably, vegetation status declined while conservation effectiveness improved from the northwestern to southeastern Amazon PAs. Moreover, PAs in the southeastern Amazon exhibited deteriorating vegetation status, i.e., increasing vulnerability with decreasing trend and stability, yet maintained significant conservation effectiveness. Focusing on PA categories, vegetation status gradually declined while conservation effectiveness continuously improved across strictly protected, not strictly protected, and indigenous-managed PA categories. Our results underscore the remarkable conservation effectiveness of Amazon PAs since 2000 and provide a theoretical basis for optimizing resource allocation and formulating policy for the Amazon basin.

title: Fragmented but greener? Bad geography promotes higher green space accessibility: evidence from 356 Chinese cities
abstract: • Natural barriers are positively linked to green space access in most Chinese cities. • Smaller cities, despite more barriers, often have better green accessibility. • Vulnerable groups face longer walking times, especially in South and East China. • Economic strength enables cities to turn geographic barriers into green assets. • Higher education levels link to lower green access in South China cities. Access to urban green spaces is a critical element of sustainable and equitable cities. However, most existing studies have primarily focused on socioeconomic inequality in green space accessibility, while the role of natural geographic constraints—such as mountains and water bodies—in shaping accessibility remains underexplored. This study bridges this gap by providing a national-scale assessment of urban park accessibility across 356 Chinese cities, integrating both geographic and socioeconomic dimensions. Using high-resolution data on park locations, residential communities, and road networks, we estimate walking and driving accessibility to urban parks through a modified three-step floating catchment area (3SFCA) model. We then measure geographic constraints in two aspects: the proportion of barriers ( share of barriers ) and the complexity of their morphology ( nonconvexity ). The results reveal that natural barriers can enhance green space accessibility under certain conditions—higher nonconvexity is associated with shorter walking times to parks (β = –1.176, p < 0.001) and higher accessibility (β = 3.348, p < 0.1). However, these effects are uneven across cities: smaller cities generally perform better due to their compact urban forms, whereas mega cities experience longer travel distances and higher inequality. The interaction between geography and economic capacity is also significant, as wealthier cities are better able to mitigate geographic constraints through infrastructure and planning. This study provides new empirical evidence that geography fundamentally influences the equity of green space access, and offers new insights for developing sustainable urban design and policy strategies in topographically diverse regions.
