title: ITC-YOLO: An improved YOLOv8 model for individual tree crown segmentation in complex forest environments
abstract: • Proposes an improved architecture ITC-YOLO, achieving an mAP50 of 93.6% in dense forests. • Achieves gains from 6.8 % to 18.2 % in mAP50 across three diverse forest biomes, compared to Mask R-CNN. • Decreases GFLOPs by 17.2 % and in parameter count by 34.4 % relative to the original YOLOv8n-seg. Individual tree crown segmentation is a critical technique for forest resource monitoring and management. Detailed monitoring at the individual tree level provides essential data to support scientifically informed forest management practices. However, state-of-the art methods remain constrained by three critical limitations: (1) insufficient segmentation accuracy in complex, dense forests, poor cross-biome generalization capability across diverse ecological environments, and unresolved trade-offs between segmentation performance and computational efficiency. To address these unresolved challenges, we proposed ITC-YOLO, an improved individual tree crown (ITC) segmentation framework developed via systematic architectural optimization of the YOLOv8-seg baseline. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of the model. For Dataset B, which corresponds to a dense forest with overlapping crowns, the proposed approach achieved an mAP50 of 93.6 %, which achieved gains ranging from 1.5 % to 8.4 % compared with the other five models. This confirms that the proposed model performs excellently for ITC segmentation in complex forest scenes. Experimental validation across three distinct forest environments further demonstrates that ITC-YOLO outperforms Mask R-CNN. Specifically, mAP50 gains are 18.2 % for the Ordos dataset covering an arid sparse forest, 8.4 % for the Hainan dataset covering a tropical rainforest, and 6.8 % for the ISPRS dataset covering a heterogeneous urban forest, respectively. Moreover, the integration of Ghost modules enables ITC-YOLO to achieve lightweight characteristics without compromising segmentation accuracy. Specifically, the model’s parameter number is reduced by 34.4 % and its computational complexity is decreased by 17.2 %. Collectively, these experimental results validate that ITC-YOLO improves segmentation accuracy, efficiency, and cross-environment adaptability, making it a robust solution for heterogeneous crown segmentation in diverse forest ecosystems.

title: Identifying city-level collaborative CO2 emissions reduction and spatio-temporal patterns: a regional perspective of the Yangtze River economic belt
abstract: • Established a framework for source–sink cities collaborative CO 2 emissions reduction. • Proposed a gravity–Fick “gravity–diffusion” index for intercity CO 2 collaboration. • Quantified and identified the degree and direction of intercity collaboration. • Revealed regional and intercity collaboration with longer distance and higher level. As climate change accelerates, it is critical to reduce CO 2 emissions equitably and efficiently. However, a unified and comparable framework for quantifying and identifying city-to-city collaborative CO 2 emission reduction (CLCER) relationships remains lacking. This gap hampers cross-city comparability, robust source–sink identification, and evidence-based allocation of collaborative reduction responsibilities, limiting the design of fair and efficient regional policies. This study examines the spatial–temporal patterns of CLCER among cities in the Yangtze River Economic Belt from 2010 to 2019. To capture both economic interactions and physical transmission mechanisms, a composite CLCER index was developed by integrating an improved gravity model with Fick’s Law of diffusion. This dual “gravity–diffusion” framework, which incorporates linear programming and the CLCER index, enables systematic identification of carbon source and sink cities while providing a balanced representation of spatial interaction and diffusion path mechanisms. The findings revealed that: (1) From 2010 to 2019, the total CLCER demand increased from 483.85 Mt to 503.52 Mt, reflecting the rising demand for cross-city collaboration driven by the strengthened differentiation of carbon source and sink cities; (2) Cities in the Central Region and Western Region, apart from cross-city offset within their own regions, accounted for 99.43 % of the Eastern Region’s CLCER demand during the study period; (3) City-level CLCER shifted towards long-distance collaboration, with average inter-city CLCER increasing from 3.75 Mt to 3.90 Mt, and the average collaborative distance expanding from 851.44 km to 983.82 km; (4) CLCER spatio-temporal patterns were characterized by growing source–sink differentiation, stronger cross-regional linkages, and more dispersed inter-city connections. This study provides insights into the relationships, degrees, and emerging patterns of CLCER, offering a framework for achieving fair and efficient regional emission reductions.

title: Assessment, driving mechanism identification and future scenario projection of desertification vulnerability in the Mongolian Plateau: an integrated study using multi-source data and machine learning
abstract: Desertification is a major ecological issue threatening sustainable development in arid and semi-arid regions globally. This study focuses on the Mongolian Plateau, employing a “assessment-attribution-prediction” framework that combines an improved MEDALUS-ESA model, interpretable machine learning, and deep learning techniques. It evaluates the spatiotemporal evolution of desertification vulnerability from 2001 to 2020, identifies key drivers, and predicts vulnerability patterns under different climate scenarios (2040–2100).The findings are as follows: (1) Desertification vulnerability on the Mongolian Plateau exhibits a clear south-to-north gradient, with an overall shift from high to low vulnerability during the study period. Very low and low vulnerability areas increased by 55320 km 2 and 94249 km 2 , respectively; (2) XGBoost-SHAP analysis identifies the bare soil index (BSI) as the most significant driver (importance of 0.2370), followed by vegetation coverage (FVC) and NDVI, with climatic factors showing pulse responses in extreme years; (3) Regional differences in drivers exist: in Inner Mongolia, vulnerability is influenced by vegetation dynamics and grazing intensity, while in Mongolia, bare land expansion, soil moisture, and grazing interact to drive vulnerability; (4) Future projections show that under different SSP scenarios, high vulnerability areas will evolve differently from 2040 to 2100, with low emission scenarios (SSP1-2.6) showing a V-shaped trend, and high emission scenarios (SSP5-8.5) leading to a continuous 8.4 % increase.

title: A Deviation-Frequency-Trend framework for multi-scale assessment of soil erosion dynamics
abstract: • Developed a DFT framework for quantifying soil erosion dynamics, overcoming traditional time-space analysis limitations. • Identified primary trajectory types of soil erosion intensity in Yunnan, highlighting key regional patterns. • Analyzed soil erosion drivers at three administrative scales, revealing scale-dependent factors. • Proposed a multi-scale erosion control strategy for “prefectures-counties-townships” levels. • The dynamic trajectory framework offers a fresh perspective on understanding complex geographic evolution. Soil erosion poses a significant threat to global ecosystem stability and sustainable development. Understanding its dynamic evolution is crucial for effective soil and water conservation management. Traditional studies often focused on single-dimensional time or spatial analyses, failing to capture the intricate spatiotemporal complexities of its evolution. To address the shortcomings, this study introduced a dynamic trajectory analysis framework based on Deviation-Frequency-Trend (DFT) to explore the spatiotemporal patterns and driving mechanisms of soil erosion intensity. Using data (1990–2022) from Yunnan Province, China, the research identified the main types of soil erosion intensity change trajectories and investigates the influence of natural and human factors across prefectures and cities, districts and counties, and townships scales. Results revealed that, (1) the most common trajectory involved “significant deviation with high-frequency decrease (SHFD)” (37.00 %), with some areas showing “significant deviation with high-frequency increase (SHFI)” (15.25 %). (2) Topography, rainfall, and vegetation cover were the main natural drivers, with their relative importance varying by scale. (3) Human factors, such as GDP growth, population pressure, and land use changes, impacted soil erosion differently at each scale. (4) Based on the spatial distribution of erosion trajectories, targeted control strategies for different regions were proposed.

title: Increases in ecosystem services in the Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau within the current century
abstract: • The increase in total ecosystem service in the QTP from 2001 to 2100. • All ecosystem services decrease significantly in permafrost regions. • Climate change and vegetation characteristic drive ecosystem service variations. • Non-permafrost regions serve as key areas for supplying ecosystem services. Global changes have profoundly affected terrestrial ecosystem services in recent decades, posing serious threats to ecological health. However, the spatial–temporal patterns and underlying drivers of ecosystem services are still lacking so far, particularly in the Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau (QTP). To address this critical gap, we assessed ecosystem services in the QTP from 2001 to 2100 by integrating six models with multi-source data. The results showed that total ecosystem service (TES) increased from northwest to southeast across the QTP. TES increased at a rate of 2.10 × 10 −3 per decade during 2001–2020 and is projected to continue increasing from 2021 to 2100 in the QTP, with rates of 2.73 × 10 −3 , 2.99 × 10 −3 , 3.85 × 10 −3 , and 3.60 × 10 −3 per decade under SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5, SSP3-7.0, and SSP5-8.5, respectively. Similar increasing trends were observed in non-permafrost regions, whereas permafrost regions exhibited opposite patterns. Annual precipitation is the primary climatic driver of TES dynamics in the QTP and non-permafrost regions, while annual precipitation and mean annual air temperature jointly influence TES changes in permafrost regions. By developing TES as a comprehensive ecological indicator, this study establishes a novel framework for long-term quantitative assessment of ecosystem services in alpine regions, providing a scientific foundation for enhancing ecological security and promoting sustainable development.

title: Trampling thresholds in dry grasslands: Cross-taxon early-warning indicators
abstract: • Both taxa lose 40–45 % cover by ∼ 100 passes and 60–65 % by 200 passes. • Abundance thresholds (richness, cover) cluster around 85–100 passes. • Vascular species composition shifts early (∼34 passes), traits only late (∼240). • Bryophyte thresholds align (∼84–104), giving early-warning signals. Recreational trampling is an emerging concern for natural dry grasslands, yet quantitative thresholds remain poorly defined. We conducted a one-year in situ trampling experiment (0–20 passes per event; up to 360 cumulative passes; one pass = one person crossing) in a natural dry grassland site and quantified vascular plant and bryophyte responses using generalised additive mixed models (GAMMs) and segmented regression. Inference was based on within-subplot change along the cumulative trampling gradient, using log-response ratios relative to baseline. Richness and cover declined non-linearly, with convergent thresholds around 85–100 passes. Vascular plants showed an early shift in species composition at ∼ 34 passes, while growth-form composition changed only at very high intensity (∼240 passes). Bryophytes responded coherently: richness (∼100), cover (∼88), species composition (∼104), and life-strategy composition (∼84) all crossed thresholds within a narrow window. Although vascular composition shifted earlier, the tighter clustering of bryophyte thresholds near management-relevant levels provides a clearer early-warning signal of trampling impacts. Even moderate off-trail use (∼85–100 cumulative passes) can trigger abrupt shifts in richness, cover, and species composition in comparable natural dry grasslands. Including bryophytes in monitoring schemes can improve the early detection of ecological tipping points under recreational use. These findings provide quantitative, management-relevant evidence to inform the conservation of natural dry grasslands, many of which in Europe are designated as Annex I habitats under the EU Habitats Directive (Natura 2000).

title: Impact of ecological restoration projects on watershed habitat quality in the Loess Plateau of China: a case study of the Yanhe River Basin
abstract: • Ecological restoration projects significantly improve the HQ in the Yanhe River Basin. • The HQ index exhibited an S-shaped trend in the Yanhe River Basin, peaking in 2010. • Using the OPGD and SEM models quantified interactive drivers of HQ. • POP and GDP were key factors affecting HQ. • Higher PRE, Slope and GDP were enhanced positive effect of NDVI on HQ. Ecological restoration projects have significantly altered the environment of China’s Loess Plateau. However, the interaction and relative importance of the underlying natural and socioeconomic drivers remain poorly understood. Thus, this study employed the Integrated Valuation of Ecosystem Services and Tradeoffs (InVEST) model, the Optimal Parameters-based Geographical Detector (OPGD) model, and Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) to assess the evolution of habitat quality (HQ) and its driving factors in the Yanhe River Basin from 1980 to 2020.The results indicate that HQ followed a sigmoidal (S-shaped) trajectory over time and exhibited significant spatial clustering (P < 0.001). It was positively correlated with the expansion of woodland and grassland but strongly negatively correlated with cultivated land and build-up land (P < 0.001). Among the drivers, population density (POP) and gross domestic product (GDP) were key factors exerting strong negative effects (path coefficients of −0.23 and −0.41, respectively), whereas the normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI) and slope showed significant positive effects (path coefficients of 0.17 and 0.23, respectively). Precipitation (PRE) indirectly improved HQ by enhancing NDVI. Furthermore, higher PRE, steeper slope, and higher GDP amplified the positive effect of NDVI, while lower PRE intensified the negative impact of human activities. In summary, ecological restoration projects markedly improved HQ in the basin, underscoring the synergistic roles of natural conditions and socioeconomic factors in shaping environmental outcomes.

title: A three-dimensional Budyko framework with terrestrial water storage dynamics: mechanistic modeling and diagnostic ecohydrological applications across global basins
abstract: • A new 3D Budyko framework incorporating water storage dynamics is developed. • The 3D model outperforms across diverse global basins compared to classical one. • The model performance is further enhanced when excluding anthropogenic impacts. • Water Storage Change Index serves as a novel ecohydrological stress indicator. The classical two-dimensional (2D) Budyko framework, while foundational for understanding water partitioning, faces critical limitations due to its steady-state assumption, which neglects terrestrial water storage changes (TWSC) and limits spatiotemporal adaptability. To address these limitations, this study advances a three-dimensional (3D) Budyko framework by incorporating TWSC derived from Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE) and Global Land Data Assimilation System (GLDAS) datasets as a dynamic third dimension, referred to as the water storage change index (WSCI). Global evaluation across diverse basins shows the 3D framework significantly outperforms both classical and extended 2D models, especially in tropical basins where accuracy improved by 55–250 %. Using GLDAS derived TWSC (excluding anthropogenic groundwater signals) further enhances the performance of the 3D Budyko framework in human-disturbed regions like the Yellow, Indus and Tigris-Euphrates basins, confirming the climate-dominated mechanism of Budyko framework. Critically, the WSCI is proved to be a powerful diagnostic ecohydrological indicator. The deviation between the observed (GRACE-based) WSCI and the climate-driven (GLDAS) baseline provides a quantitative measure of the anthropogenic distortion of the natural water cycle. Moreover, the spatial association analysis between WSCI and Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), using Local Indicators of Spatial Association (LISA) method, further validated its ecological relevance. It reveals distinct patterns of ecohydrological coupling across global diverse basins, including natural synergy (sufficient water availability supporting healthy vegetation), natural stress (water scarcity co-occurring with limited vegetation), and critically, human-induced unsustainability where high vegetation greenness coexists with water storage depletion. This 3D Budyko framework not only improves prediction accuracy but also offers a mechanistic tool for monitoring ecological water stress and guiding sustainable water management under climate and anthropogenic pressures.

title: Temporal comparison of coral reefs in the Galápagos using differential alignment of 3D models and Machine-Learning
abstract: Underwater photogrammetry is a popular tool for coral community surveys, however, comparing 3D maps over time requires a complicated set of operations. Primarily, it is difficult to align dynamic scenes in order to visualize and measure changes because different components in the map move in different directions and rates. Moreover, analyzing 3D maps for coral community structure involves image annotation which is laborious and requires expert knowledge. Here, we use differential alignment and Model Assisted Labeling to solve the aforementioned problems. Instead of aligning our full maps, we crop them into sub-parts and align them separately enabling us to copy the location of 3D survey points between years and conduct a direct pointwise comparison. To annotate the points, we used classifications from a deep neural net trained by us and reviewed by a human annotator, resulting in substantial time savings. Our results show that differential alignment is effective for 3D model registration over time, and that although our classifier reached precision values typically around 60 percent for key classes, this was efficient in expediting the annotation process. We perform a pointwise temporal comparison of benthic composition and examine key ecological indicators including percent coral cover, coral diversity, and structural complexity. The results show that while structural complexity decreased over time, coral cover showed site specific trends warranting further research in the region to determine how these changes may affect reef resilience and recovery.

title: A generalizable deep learning framework for large-scale mapping of seagrass habitats
abstract: Abstract Seagrass meadows play a vital role in supporting coastal communities by promoting biodiversity, mitigating coastal erosion and contributing to local economies. These ecosystems face significant threats, including habitat loss and degradation or climate change. United Nations has recognized the urgency of conserving marine ecosystems, highlighting the need for evidence-based conservation strategies and high-quality monitoring. However, traditional monitoring approaches are often time-consuming, labor-intensive, and costly, limiting their scalability and effectiveness. The growing availability of remote sensing data coupled to the rise of machine learning technologies offer an unprecedented opportunity to develop autonomous, efficient and scalable monitoring systems. Despite many efforts, the development of such systems for seagrass meadows remains a challenge, with recent attempts presenting several limitations such as limited satellite imagery, inadequate metrics for evaluating model performance or insufficient ground truth data, leading to simple proof of concepts rather than useful solutions. Here, we overcome these limitations by developing a comprehensive framework to map Posidonia oceanica meadows in the Mediterranean Sea using an extensive georeferenced habitat dataset and diverse satellite imagery for model training. We successfully evaluate the model generalization capability across different regions and provide the trained model for broader application in biodiversity monitoring and management.

title: Spectral indices to evaluate the physiological response of Mediterranean shrubs to browsing
abstract: • Herbivory influences the physiological and spectral response of plants. • Plant palatability affected spectral and physiological indicators. • R750/R800 and R740/R800 indices were effective in detecting deer herbivory. • Some spectral and physiological indices showed great seasonal variation. • Spectral indices are useful for management of herbivore-dominated systems. Herbivory by large ungulates may cause important physiological and spectral changes in plants, which may serve as ecological indicators of herbivore overabundance. This study examines the physiological and spectral response of plants to recent and prolonged browsing through remote sensing techniques. We selected 30 plants from two Mediterranean shrub species with contrasting palatability: Cistus ladanifer (non-palatable) and Phillyrea angustifolia (highly palatable). Plants were subjected to three treatments: 1) no browsing (deer exclosure), 2) simulated recent browsing (clipping 30% of branchlets), and 3) intense, long-life natural browsing by deer ( Cervus elaphus ). Leaf physiological variables (chlorophyll, flavonols, anthocyanins, Nitrogen Balance Index (NBI), chlorophyll fluorescence, and stomatal conductance) were measured, and 27 spectral indices were calculated from reflectance data. The less herbivore-adapted Cistus showed lower chlorophyll (−27.7%), nitrogen (−26.8%), and stomatal conductance (−19.24%) when browsed compared to non-browsed plants, while no differences were found in the more palatable Phillyrea . Reflectance indices R750 / R800 and R740 / R800 related with chlorophyll fluorescence, were significantly lower for the intense, long-life browsing treatment in both species. Other indices such as R690 / R600 only showed significant differences between species. NDPI and SRPI indices, related to carotenoid/chlorophyll ratio, showed seasonally variable responses to browsing, with higher levels in spring for both herbivory treatments. We conclude that some spectral indices related to chlorophyll/carotenoids were able to detect physiological stress from deer herbivory, with key seasonal and species-specific variations for both, palatable and non-palatable shrubs. This demonstrates the potential and context-dependent use of spectral indices for the ecology and management of herbivore-dominated environments.

title: Integrating multi-temporal information for monitoring plant spectral diversity with PlanetScope and Sentinel-2 satellite imagery
abstract: Plant diversity is important for the conservation and management of forest ecosystems. Satellite remote sensing data provides a time-efficient and large-scale approach of monitoring plant diversity with spectral diversity. The relationship between spectral and plant diversity varied by time, but most studies failed to integrate multi-temporal information into spectral diversity metrics. Moreover, the consistency of spectral diversity metrics remains poorly understood. This study conducted a systematic comparison of five commonly used spectral diversity metrics, including coefficient of variation (CV), spectral angle mapper (SAM), spectral information divergence (SID), spectral α-diversity (SD α ), and convex hull volume (CHV). Based on time-series PlanetScope satellite imagery and in-situ plant species data obtained from four National Ecological Observatory Network (NEON) field sites, we first validated the feasibility of an innovative approach for monitoring species diversity with spectral diversity by integrating multi-temporal information. We then applied the multi-temporal spectral diversity metrics to the subtropical evergreen forests in southern China using time-series Sentinel-2 satellite imagery, and compared the consistency of the spectral diversity metrics. Our results showed that the multi-temporal spectral diversity metrics significantly improved the performance in monitoring plant species diversity compared to the mono-temporal metrics (R 2 = 0.21–0.38). CV, SAM, SID, SD α , and CHV exhibited significant correlations at all time points ( p < 0.001), but the extreme values in December led to a significant decrease in the correlations particularly for SD α and CHV. The multi-temporal spectral diversity metrics were significantly correlated with those calculated based on mono-temporal Sentinel-2 data ( p < 0.001), although the effects of temporal information on the correlations varied by spectral diversity metrics. The newly proposed spectral diversity metrics can capture the temporal variation in vegetation spectra, and demonstrated strong potential and feasibility for monitoring plant diversity. This study expands the perspective of spectral diversity applications by incorporating multiple temporal information, and provides valuable insights for large-scale biodiversity monitoring with satellite remote sensing.

title: Structural model sensitivity alters predictions and affects management decision-making ability
abstract: AbstractEcological modelling is increasingly used to predict the consequences of environmental management under global change, but is difficult to develop and test and poor models can lead to real-world environmental and societal harm. Model structure (i.e., how the system is represented) can contribute significant uncertainty. Here, we analyse structural choices in a widely-used model linking hydrological indicators to environmental outcomes in the Murray-Darling Basin, Australia. We assess the sensitivity of modelled outcomes to the shape of relationships (e.g., linear vs. nonlinear) and choices of aggregation methods in space, time, and ecological groupings. Comparing outcomes within a single ‘historical’ scenario, outcomes ranged from very low to very high ecological condition based solely on a simple set of modelling choices. Relationship shape, aggregation functions, when aggregation functions were applied, and the length of time over which assessments were made were all highly influential. Comparing 12 climate and management scenarios, sensitivity depended on the amount of water and the distribution of values being aggregated. Common default choices (e.g., linear relationships and arithmetic means) were not necessarily conservative and may inflate risk. Common approaches to reduce structural uncertainty, such as ensemble modelling or comparing scenarios, were only partially successful. We recommend grouping by the type of ecological response (e.g., threshold vs. linear) to balance parsimony and realism, as well as separately reporting several competing structures. Uncritical use of a single structure represents the highest risk of poor decision-making. Explicit testing and reporting of structural uncertainty is essential for robust, science-based environmental management.

title: Spatiotemporal variations and drivers of water quality in the source region of the Yellow River
abstract: Structural equation modelling (SEM) results, showing the interactions between environmental factors (topography, land use types, and climate) and water quality parameters. The red and blue lines indicate positive and negative effects, respectively, while arrows between nodes indicate causal relationships. Thicker lines/arrows indicate stronger causal effects. Darker edges indicate a higher significance level ( p ≤ 0.05). H, TWI, DO, EC, PMI, and TN denote the mean elevation, topographic wetness index, dissolved oxygen, electrical conductivity, permanganate index, and total nitrogen, respectively. • Topography, land use types, and hydroclimatic parameters affect the water quality. • Hydroclimatic and biogeochemical processes shape the seasonality of water quality. • Elevation and TWI have a synergistic influence on land use and water quality in the SRYR. The source region of the Yellow River (SRYR) plays a critical role in runoff formation and ecological function in the Yellow River Basin. However, comprehensive research on water quality in this basin remains relatively scarce. Exploring water quality across different spatial regions of the basin is, in fact, important for ensuring sustainable development in the region. In this context, the present study aims to assess the spatiotemporal variations in water quality in the SRYR in September 2021 and June 2022 using the Wilcoxon test, Spearman correlation analysis, clustering, and principal component analysis (PCA). The clustering results classified the water quality in the SRYR into three regions. The spatial variability in the water quality across the relatively undisturbed upper and middle reaches of the region was primarily governed by topographic features and land use types. In contrast, anthropogenic disturbances from agricultural activities and urbanization in the lower basin promoted the formation of biogeochemical hotspots, marked by high topographic wetness index values as well as elevated concentrations of organic matter, and heavy metals. Cluster analysis coupled with PCA revealed the major factors driving water quality in the study area. On the other hand, the structural equation model results indicated that climatic variables, such as temperature, have moderate effects on water quality. Specifically, hydrological transport processes (e.g., discharge rate) increased the concentrations of total nitrogen, total phosphorus, turbidity and selenium, but decreased the concentrations of nutrients and organic substances through dilution effects at the basin scale. This study highlights the significance of reducing agricultural expansion and implementing sustained water quality and hydroclimatic monitoring policies to effectively protect and predict water quality, enabling the development of proactive strategies to mitigate the effects of increasingly extreme and variable climate regimes.

title: New insights on sustainable energy security of China based on a double-frontier network data envelopment analysis
abstract: • Developing a novel framework for evaluating system performance using two indices. • Proposing improved network data envelopment analysis models for index evaluation. • China’s sustainable energy security (SES) index exhibited a trend of fluctuating growth. • The regional energy system demonstrated considerable potentials for SES improvement. • The regional energy system confronted risks related to energy transition and energy supply. The energy system’s security and efficiency are core to sustainable development. However, traditional evaluations of its performance often overlook the interplay between these two dimensions. To address this gap, this study proposes a novel framework integrating two complementary indices, i.e., the Sustainable Energy Security (SES) and Overall Performance Loss (OES) indices, to jointly assess energy system performance. Methodologically, two advanced network Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) models are developed. The SES index quantifies multi-stage collaborative efficiency and stage-specific input–output efficiency from the traditional DEA efficiency perspective, while the OES index innovatively captures performance potential and risk by integrating dual optimistic and pessimistic DEA frontiers. This framework is applied to evaluate China’s provincial energy systems from 2018 to 2022. The results show that: (1) China’s SES index exhibited a fluctuating upward trend, with the western region taking the lead; (2) Significant provincial spatial disparities in SES index were observed, as demarcated by the Heihe-Tengchong line, and resource-based provinces retained relative advantages; (3) The OES index identified moderate risks of performance loss in some provinces with high SES values, though such risks are not highly pronounced; (4) Most provinces were categorized as either “Low efficiency with low risk (L-L)” or “High efficiency with low risk (H-L)”. In conclusion, proactively mitigating potential risks is vital to optimizing energy system sustainability and facilitating the sustainable energy transition.

title: Local scale assessment of peatland restoration priorities using multi-sensor airborne remote sensing and machine learning
abstract: • Multi-sensor airborne data support monitoring of peatlands at a local scale. • Peatland plant communities mapped into 22 classes with 79% overall accuracy. • Novel desiccation index quantifies short-term peatland desiccation (∼16 % RMSE, ∼12.5 % MAE) • Bog-type peatlands show lowest resilience, fen-type peatlands show highest. • Results identify priority sites for targeted peatland restoration actions. Advances in remote sensing now enable comprehensive monitoring of peatlands, providing detailed data on vegetation composition and hydrological conditions. The main objective of this study was to assess the potential of multi-sensor airborne data for monitoring the short-term drought resilience of peat-forming vegetation at the local scale. The study covered 248 peatlands within the Tuchola Forest (northern Poland), for which three types of airborne data were acquired in 2022 using sensor fusion: LiDAR, hyperspectral, and thermal imagery, along with ground-based reference data. Machine learning techniques were applied to develop: (a) a map of peatland plant communities comprising 22 legend classes, which achieved an overall accuracy of 79 %, and (b) a spatial desiccation model of peatland vegetation − constructed for a selected subset of eight peatlands − based on the novel Multifactorial Peatland Desiccation Index. The model achieved a Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) of 1.898 (∼16 %) and a Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 1.536 (∼12.5 %). Classification results revealed that non-peat-forming vegetation types cover nearly 67 % of the delineated peatland area, reflecting its degradation. Analysis of desiccation across peat-forming plant communities shows that the lowest short-term drought resilience is observed in Ledo-Sphagnetum magellanici and Sphagno recurvi-Eriophoretum vaginati communities, typical of bog-type peatlands. In contrast, the highest resilience was found in Scorpidio-Caricetum diandrae and Menyantho-Sphagnetum teretis communities, characteristic of fen-type peatlands. Assessment of the extent and desiccation status of valuable peat-forming communities enabled the identification of peatlands for highest-priority restoration.

title: Spatiotemporal patterns and driving mechanisms of critical soil moisture thresholds in Chinese ecosystems
abstract: • θ crit declines in most climatic zones, but rises in NW and QTP. • Land-use types showed varied θ crit trends, may reflecting different water-use efficiency. • VPD controls θ crit in arid zones, while PPT governs it in humid regions. • θ crit became more sensitive to PPT but less sensitive to VPD over time. Global climate change is profoundly reshaping the hydrological cycles of ecosystems worldwide, heightening the need to understand how these systems respond to shifts in ecohydrological processes. A key indicator in this regard is the critical soil moisture threshold ( θ crit ), which marks the transition from unstressed plant water use to moisture-limited conditions. This study provides a systematic analysis of the spatiotemporal patterns of θ crit across diverse ecosystems in China from 1980 to 2020. Our findings reveal a general decline in θ crit across most ecosystem types over this period. Notably, however, in northwest China and the Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau, θ crit exhibited an increasing trend, contrasting with declines observed in other climate zones. At the land-use level, θ crit decreased in most classifications, with the exception of Open Shrublands and Barren areas. The mechanistic analysis identified that vapor pressure deficit dominated the θ crit variations in arid and semi-arid zones, while precipitation was the primary factor in more humid regions. In the Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau, solar radiation had a primary negative impact on θ crit . In the subtropical or tropical humid south of China, the water deficit index was the main negative driver. A comparative analysis reveals a marked shift in the influences of key climatic drivers on the θ crit between the two periods (1980–2000 and 2001–2020). The positive effect of precipitation was enhanced, while the inhibitory effect of vapor pressure deficit was reduced. Concurrently, the sensitivity of θ crit to both water deficit and actual evapotranspiration declined across most regions, suggesting a weakening influence of these factors. Moreover, the negative effect of maximum temperature intensified notably in northern and northwestern China, likely due to enhanced soil moisture depletion and increased atmospheric evaporative demand under warmer conditions. This study provided a theoretical framework for assessing ecosystem adaptability and informing water resource management.

title: Carbon reduction and water resource trade-offs in the digital-green synergistic transformation
abstract: • Digital-Green Synergistic Transformation (DGST) exhibits an inverted U-shaped effect on carbon emissions, revealing the necessity of adaptive policies. • DGST induces an inverted U-shaped carbon–water trade-off, with initial conflicts most evident in regions east of the China and in water-scarce areas. • Significant spatial spillovers of DGST affect carbon emissions and trade-offs, emphasizing coordinated cross-regional governance. The Digital-green synergistic transformation (DGST) constitutes a critical pathway for addressing climate change and advancing sustainable development. This paper examines the impact of DGST on carbon emissions and its associated environmental trade-offs, drawing on panel data from 280 Chinese cities. The results reveal a significant nonlinear relationship between DGST and carbon emissions, characterized by an inverted U-shaped pattern. This effect is more pronounced in regions located east of the China and in areas with abundant water resources. From a coupled resource system perspective, the analysis further identifies a carbon–water trade-off during the early stages of transformation, wherein carbon reductions are accompanied by increased water consumption. This trade-off is particularly evident in cities east of the China and in water-stressed regions. Spatial econometric analysis reveals significant spatial autocorrelation in carbon emissions, suggesting that DGST is associated with spatial spillover effects on carbon emissions and related trade-offs across regions. This paper contributes to the theoretical understanding of the mechanisms underlying carbon mitigation within the context of DGST and provides empirical insights to inform multi-objective environmental governance and policy formulation.

title: Time-series reconstruction and mapping of forest aboveground biomass in the Great Xing’an Mountains of China using GEDI, MODIS, and machine learning
abstract: Accurate long-term estimation of forest aboveground biomass (AGB) is essential for understanding carbon dynamics and assessing the impacts of climate change and human disturbance. However, generating high-resolution, continuous AGB time series remains challenging due to data limitations and methodological constraints. In this study, we present a 21-year (2000–2020) reconstruction of forest AGB in China’s Great Xing’an Mountains by integrating multi-temporal MODIS imagery with spaceborne LiDAR data from the GEDI L4B product using the AutoGluon stacking ensemble learning algorithm. All models achieved root mean square errors (RMSE) below 25 Mg/ha, with weighted ensemble model yielding superior performance (R 2 = 0.83, RMSE = 13.99 Mg/ha, rRMSE = 14.38 %). Trend analysis based on Sen’s slope and the Mann-Kendall test revealed a significant regional increase in AGB, with 83.36 % of forest area exhibiting upward trends, while 16.64 % showed declines. Fire disturbance emerged as a primary driver of localized AGB loss, particularly in the northern and eastern subregions. From 2000 to 2020, average forest AGB increased by 14.67 Mg/ha, and total biomass rose by 0.53 Pg. These results demonstrate the potential of combining GEDI and MODIS data with machine learning for large-scale, long-term forest biomass monitoring, offering valuable support for carbon accounting, ecological assessment, and forest management in cold-temperate ecosystems.

title: Dynamic multi-criteria analysis of water resources carrying capacity under anthropogenic pressure
abstract: • Multi-method framework (AHP–Entropy–CRITIC–game theory) ensured balanced WRCC weighting. • WRCC (2012–2021) showed mostly critical, overloaded states under hydro-anthropic stress. • Upstream allocation, inflow quality, and supply–demand balance were key WRCC drivers. • ARIMA performed well for socio-economic data, but water quality needs hybrid modeling. • Integrated strategies sustain long-term ecological and socio-economic balance in the region. Water resources underpin ecological sustainability, human well-being, and socio-economic development, yet their sustainable management remains a global challenge. This study presents a comprehensive assessment of the Water Resources Carrying Capacity (WRCC) of the Anzali Wetland in northern Iran, integrating system dynamics modelling, multi-method indicator weighting, cloud-based evaluation, obstacle factor analysis, and ARIMA forecasting. Eleven key indicators, reflecting hydrological, socio-economic, and environmental drivers, were selected through expert consultation. Their relative importance was quantified by combining Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP), Entropy, and CRITIC methods, and optimized via game-theoretic integration to ensure a balanced and objective weighting framework. WRCC evaluation for 2012–2021 using the cloud model revealed persistent critical and overloaded states, with transient improvements in certain years and noticeable effects from the COVID-19 pandemic. Obstacle factor analysis identified upstream water allocation, urban population growth, and agricultural water use efficiency as the dominant constraints. ARIMA-based forecasts for 2022–2031, coupled with scenario analysis, demonstrated that integrated management, combining wetland expansion, improved inflow water quality, and enhanced irrigation efficiency, offers the most robust pathway for long-term WRCC sustainability. These findings provide a replicable methodological framework and actionable insights for wetland conservation and water resource management under complex socio-ecological pressures.

title: Potential use of multi-year UAV imagery for monitoring vegetation traits in grasslands
abstract: • UAV-based vegetation traits monitoring clearly demonstrates changes in managed grasslands. • Changes in vegetation traits, especially C:N ratios, allow differentiation of management intensity. • Estimating vegetation traits from multi-annual UAV data is challenged by radiometric inconsistencies. • Site-specific spatiotemporal analysis of vegetation traits provides valuable insights for grassland management. Permanent grasslands in Germany are characterized by the intensity of management practices. The intensity of management significantly influences both the biodiversity and ecosystem services provided by grasslands. Therefore, monitoring vegetation traits of intensively managed grasslands is crucial for making management decisions aimed at maximizing ecosystem services and minimizing environmental footprints of grassland cultivation. In intensively managed grasslands, aboveground dry biomass (AGB dry ), plant species richness, vegetation carbon (C) and nitrogen (N) content, and carbon to nitrogen (C:N) ratio serve as key indicators to assess the condition of the grassland, an information which is highly relevant for farmers, inspectors, and decision-makers. This study aimed to accurately estimate AGB dry , N, C:N ratio, plant species richness, and Shannon H-index in two study areas in Bavaria, Germany using multi-year in-situ measurements and corresponding unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) imagery. The combined in situ and UAV dataset was collected at different grassland sites (Fendt, Rottenbuch, and Bayreuth area) between 2019 and 2023, partly at several times during one year. Therefore, the dataset covers both intra- and inter-annual growth patterns (April to October). UAV images were radiometrically calibrated using a reflectance target and processed with Pix4D’s internal radiometric corrections. Both Random Forest and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) were used to estimate grassland traits. The regression models were trained using the in-situ measurements, and as predictor variables the corresponding reflectance in the spectral bands of the multispectral UAV imagery and the derived vegetation indices. Model performance was assessed using an independent validation dataset, consisting of 20 % of the reference data that were not included in the model training stage. To improve estimation accuracy, we conducted test cases by training the regression models using different training data subsets. As a result, we derived multi-year vegetation trait maps from UAV imagery with R 2 values of 0.81 for AGB dry , 0.77 for N content, 0.81 for the C:N ratio, 0.84 for SR and 0.86 for H-index, respectively. Overall, the study highlights the potential of integrating multi-year in situ data with UAV imagery to create multidimensional datasets that effectively capture spatial and temporal changes in vegetation traits.

title: The interactive effects of damming and urbanization on multitrophic aquatic communities in a highly populated watershed in China
abstract: • Dam and urbanization interaction increased nutrient and heavy metal concentrations. • Stressors’s interaction reduced aquatic biodiversity and food web stability. • Stressors’ interaction shifted community from clean to pollution-tolerant species. • The ecological impacts of locating dams in urban areas should be carefully assessed. • Macroinvertebrates biodiversity were crucial in disturbing environments. Damming and urbanization, the two most common anthropogenic pressures worldwide, have caused fundamental changes in aquatic habitats and the species they support. Although these two stressors frequently cooccur, their interactive effects on aquatic communities have not been specifically investigated. Here, we investigated multitrophic aquatic communities, including macroinvertebrate, zooplankton and algae communities, in the Shaying River Basin to reveal the interactive effects of damming and urbanization on biodiversity, food web stability and community structure. We found that the cooccurrence of damming and urbanization led to a significant decline in the diversity indices of all aquatic communities and in food web stability, mainly through synergistic effects. Structural equation modeling (SEM) revealed that both direct pathways and indirect pollutant-mediated pathways, including the accumulation of nutrients (N, P) and heavy metals (As, Cr, Fe, Zn), contributed to this decline and ultimately simplified the freshwater food webs. Macroinvertebrate diversity plays a crucial role in the maintenance of food web stability. In addition, nonmetric multidimensional scaling (NMDS) and variance partitioning analysis (VPA) indicated that the interaction of damming and urbanization caused significant homogenization among macroinvertebrates, zooplankton, and algae. As stress increased, the dominant species shifted from pollution-sensitive species (e.g., Ephemeroplera , Trichoptera and Ploima ) to pollution-tolerant species (e.g., Diptera and Tubificida ). Our results suggest that damming and urbanization together exert strong environmental filtering effects, which significantly reshape freshwater community structures.

title: An integrated framework for monitoring and predicting coastal land subsidence: a case study of Xiamen, China
abstract: • Integrated coastal subsidence framework: monitoring, risk assessment and prediction. • Novel indicators are designed to assess coastal subsidence risk. • Fusion model outperforms three base models in coastal subsidence prediction. Land subsidence in coastal areas poses significant threats, including geological disasters, seawater intrusion, and degradation of coastal wetlands. This paper presents a comprehensive research framework for monitoring, assessing, and predicting land subsidence in coastal areas. Utilizing Sentinel-1A imagery and leveling survey data acquired from May 2017 to December 2023, combined with multiple predictive models, this framework was applied to Xiamen City, China. Our findings reveal that: (1) the main subsidence velocity in Xiamen ranged from −12.5 to 7.5 mm/yr, with Xiang’an District experiencing the most significant subsidence, and Huli District the least; (2) We divided Land Subsidence Risk (LSR) into five grades, identifying 65.37 km 2 (5.73 % of the total assessment area) as higher risk, predominating in Haicang District, Jimei District, Tong’an District, and Siming District; (3) The LSR of Xiamen Island and Dadeng Island needs special attention, due to their economic importance and the ongoing infrastructure projects, respectively; (4) Model performance analysis indicated that the Informer model outperformed eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) model and Seasonal AutoRegressive Integrated Moving Average (SARIMA) model with the fusion model further enhancing prediction accuracy. These findings offer a scientific basis for land subsidence mitigation and support decision-making for enhancing urban resilience and coastal zone management.

title: Evaluation of nature-based solutions’ contributions to the sustainable development goals
abstract: • A novel framework using expert scoring of multi-indicators and causal relations is proposed for NbS ∼ SDG linkages. • Governance, gender equality, and education require to be included in NbS monitoring frameworks. • Current NbS interventions primarily contribute to either environmental, social, or economic rather than accounting for the multidimensional benefits. • Sectoral silos and trade-offs among environmental, social, and economic benefits emphasize the need to implement complementary NbS for sustainable development. Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) are key metric to evaluate the multifaceted outcomes of Nature-based Solutions (NbS). However, existing frameworks for analyzing the NbS contributions largely focus on environmental and societal domain, undermining all the associated contributions to the SDGs, and fail to account for their broader national impact. The present study applied a novel mixed-method approach to assess contributions of NbS to the SDGs, by considering the NbS implemented in Central India. The analyzed 87 number of articles, selected through a systematic review, classified 39 identified NbS into 11 broader categories, claiming contribution to all the 17 SDGs. However, further analysis revealed discrepancies between such theoretical claims and real-world implementation. An expert panel of fourteen stakeholders from diverse disciplines scored 39 NbS interventions against their contributions toward the 17 SDGs. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) identified underlying patterns in expert perceptions on NbS contributions revealing four distinct groups, indicating that most of the NbS interventions primarily contribute to one or two sustainability dimensions i.e. environmental, social, or economic, rather than delivering the multidimensional benefits. Subsequently, the relationships observed between NbS and their contributions to SDGs through Structural Equation Modelling (SEM) reinforced PCA findings by revealing non-significant interactions among the four defined aspects of sustainability: ‘environmental’, ‘social’, ‘economic’, and the ‘other’. The results highlight persistent sectoral silos in intervention implementation strategies and potential trade-offs that hinder the intended cross-sectoral benefits of NbS. Effective acceleration of SDG achievement requires stronger integration of local NbS interventions with active community participation. The multi-pronged methodology provided an informative and cost-effective assessment. Future research should prioritize multi-stakeholder assessment and empirical impact evaluations to guide metric-based policy adoption for socio-economic and environmental sustainability through NbS.

title: Precipitation facilitates reversal of grassland degradation and desertification in drylands of Xinjiang
abstract: • Grasslands in Xinjiang show a continuous greening trend from 2000 to 2022. • The grassland-desert transition zone, which accounts for 14% of the Xinjiang. • Precipitation as a major driver of grassland degradation and desertification reversal. Grassland (GRA) degradation and desertification have become global ecological challenges that severely threaten the achievement of Sustainable Development Goal 15.3 (SDG 15.3). Understanding the processes of GRA degradation and desertification is crucial for developing effective restoration policies, especially in ecologically vulnerable drylands. On the basis of desertification dynamics and vegetation growth characteristics, we delineated the permanent GRA zone (PGZ), GRA − desert transition zone (TZ), and permanent desert zone (PDZ). Afterwards, the effects of climatic and anthropogenic factors on GRA degradation and desertification were quantified. The results revealed that GRA showed a consistent greening trend across all zones in Xinjiang. The TZ covers 14 % of the area, with severe degradation (44 %) concentrated along the TZ–PDZ boundary and declining stepwise towards the PGZ. The PGZ covers 12 %, and the PDZ covers 74 %. From 2013 to 2022, the reversal of GRA desertification occurred mainly in the oasis regions of the Junggar Basin, northern Tianshan Basin, and Tarim Basin peripheries. The GRA centroid shifted 89.51 km from southeastern Tacheng to southern Ili Kazakh Autonomous Prefecture. GeoDetector analysis revealed that precipitation (q = 0.45) was the key driver of GRA degradation and desertification reversal. Interaction analysis revealed that precipitation enhanced CO 2 effects (q = 0.65), amplified population density on plains (q = 0.63), strengthened temperature effects in mountains (q = 0.66), and reinforced livestock effects in the PGZ. Reversing GRA degradation and desertification under warm, wet conditions has the potential to improve fragile arid ecosystems, providing insights for ecological protection and desertification control.

title: Evaluating the impact of urban expansion on ecosystem carbon based on a long time series 30 m resolution NPP dataset
abstract: • Urban expansion reduced vegetation NPP by 13.77 % in CZT from 2000 to 2020. • Direct LULC changes contributed 54.62 % to NPP loss in CZT. • Heat island effect negatively impacted vegetation NPP in CZT. Urban areas significantly influence the natural environment and play a critical role in the global carbon cycle. Quantifying the impact of urban expansion on carbon stocks is essential for assessing vegetation dynamics and regional carbon balance. This study analyzes the spatiotemporal evolution of vegetation net primary productivity (NPP) in the Chang-Zhu-Tan (CZT) urban agglomeration from 2000 to 2020 using high-resolution (30 m) Landsat NDVI, land use/land cover (LULC), and meteorological data within the CASA model. Key findings reveal that the annual mean vegetation NPP ranged between 246 and 356 g C/m 2 a −1 , with higher values in peripheral areas and lower values in urban centers. Approximately 20.01 % of the region experienced significant decreases in NPP, while only 10.11 % showed increases. Urban expansion was responsible for 13.77 % of the total NPP loss relative to the base year (2000), with pronounced reductions in eastern Changsha and urban confluences. Furthermore, direct drivers (e.g., LULC changes) contributed 54.62 % to NPP loss, while indirect factors (e.g., climate change) accounted for 45.38 %. These results underscore the dual influence of direct and indirect anthropogenic factors on carbon dynamics in rapidly urbanizing regions.

title: Multiscale coordination dynamics in large freshwater lake basin ecosystems: machine learning reveals spatiotemporal variations and driving mechanisms of risk–quality–service process interactions
abstract: Large freshwater lake basins face dual pressures from human activity and ecological degradation. However, the mechanisms driving coordinated ecosystem development through interactions among ecological risk (ER), environmental quality (EQ), and ecosystem services (ES) remain unclear. To address this gap, this study developed a composite index of ecosystem coordinated development level (ECDL) by integrating the ER–EQ–ES subsystems using the coupling coordination degree Model (CCDM). Integrating exploratory spatiotemporal data analysis (ESTDA), multiscale geographically and temporally weighted regression (MGTWR), Pearson correlation, and machine learning algorithms, spatiotemporal variations in ECDL and its multidimensional environmental drivers were explored. A multiscale analysis across the Dongting Lake basin, sub-basins, and grid levels between 2000, 2010, and 2020 revealed that ER increasingly concentrated in lake-dense areas, while EQ and ES showed sustained growth in inland forest regions. ECDL remained stable in upstream sub-basins, whereas downstream urban clusters exhibited lower and more fragmented coordination. Coldspots in suburban agricultural belts and lakefront plains consistently suppressed ECDL. ER imposed negative constraints on ECDL, with sub-basin MGTWR coefficients as low as –0.26. EQ was enhanced in high ECDL clustering, with sub-basin coefficients reaching 0.34. ES showed strong local sensitivity. Pearson correlation revealed generally positive associations between natural environments (NE) and ECDL (r > 0.60), but negative correlations with anthropogenic (AE) and composite environments (CE). XGBoost–SHAP analysis uncovered nonlinear interactions where NE promoted, AE suppressed, and CE constrained ECDL. Response mechanisms of individual factors varied significantly across sub-basins. NE dominated in western ecological barrier zones, modulated by CE. Leaf area index and land diversity showed threshold effects at normalized values of 0.30 and 0.50. In southern urban–agricultural transition zones, AE progressively inhibited NE’s regulatory role. In eastern water-intensive zones, AE’s suppressive effect weakened as NE’s regulatory function recovered. This study overcomes single-scale or model limitations by highlighting scale-dependent and environmental threshold effects of ECDL, offering insights to support SDGs 6,11, and 15.

title: Quantifying the contribution of urbanization to temperature rise based on tree-ring density data in northern hemisphere
abstract: • Tree-ring MXD was applied to quantify urbanization’s contribution to warming. • Tree-ring MXD was significantly correlated with temperature at interannual scales. • UCR exhibited pronounced regional contrasts across continents. Urbanization is a major non-climatic factor influencing temperature, and quantifying its contribution is essential for disentangling natural and anthropogenic drivers of recent warming. Based on the fifty-nine tree-ring maximum latewood density (MXD) datasets (as a natural reference unaffected by urbanization) in Northern Hemisphere and Climatic Research Unit (CRU) gridded temperature datasets from adjacent urban areas, we systematically examined discrepancies between them in the long-term trends. The results indicated that the tree-ring MXD is correlated significantly with temperature at the interannual scale (first-order differencing correlation coefficient 0.635 ± 0.112), while the rates of tree-ring growth were generally lower than the pace of urban warming over annual to decadal time scales, particularly in Americas and Asia, which are substantially influenced by urbanization. We estimated the urbanization contribution rate (UCR) for the Northern Hemisphere based on the difference in linear trends between temperature and tree-ring MXD. UCR averaged 75.26 % in Northern Hemisphere, with the highest regional mean value in Americas (81.85 %), followed by Europe (75.68 %) and Asia (66.73 %). The results indicated that the tree-ring MXD could be used as a natural proxy independent of urbanization influence. We provide a new approach for quantifying the potential bias caused by the urban heat island (UHI) effect. The approach not only helps refine assessments of global warming but also offers a new explanation for the reduced sensitivity of recent tree growth to temperature at high northern latitudes.

title: Quantifying realized ecosystem services from the supply-flow-demand perspective and understanding the management implications: a case study of the Chengdu Prefecture, China
abstract: • A realized ecosystem service (ES) evaluation framework was proposed. • The realized ESs and ES supplies of crop pollination, flood regulation and natural recreation showed different distributions. • The trade-offs/synergies of realized ES pairs help managers avoid overestimating the ES synergy. • The ES management zone scheme is influenced by the adoption of the realized ES or ES supply in bundle analysis. • The hotspot of the realized ES can identify the areas crucial for providing the actual benefit. To efficiently improve human wellbeing by managing ecosystem services (ESs), decision-makers have shown more interest in how many ESs are used by humans (realized service, RS) over how many ESs are provided by ecosystems (service supply, SS). However, the RS is determined by ecosystems, social systems and their complex interactions simultaneously, so RS evaluation is still challenging. In this study, we constructed an RS evaluation framework from the supply-flow-demand perspective, and applied this framework to four typical ESs in the Chengdu Prefecture, China. We quantified the SS and RS of the four ESs, and then compared the trade-offs/synergies and hotspots of the SS and RS to discuss how the RS adoption influences management decision-making. Our results show that: (1) Except for carbon sequestration, the SS and RS of the other three ESs exhibited different distributions. (2) For ES synergies/trade-offs, all the ES pairs showed synergies from the SS perspective, while such synergies were weakened or even converted into trade-offs from the RS perspective. This implies the risk of overrating ES synergies based on the SS. Moreover, the SS and RS bundles showed different distributions and ES compositions, which indicated that the ES management zoning scheme (including spatial layout and management strategies) formulated with the SS will be changed when RSs are management targets. (3) SS and RS hotspots exhibited different spatial patterns, and only less than half of SS hotspots were identified as RS hotspots. The RS adaptation in ES hotspot analysis can help identify the areas crucial for providing actual benefits as the conservation priority. This study can not only deepen the understanding of actual natural contributions to humans, but can also support ES management aimed at human wellbeing improvement.

title: Prioritizing vegetation restoration potential to facilitate snow leopard habitat recovery in Sanjiangyuan region
abstract: • 18 % of snow leopard habitat degraded, with 69% in medium to high suitability zones. • Matching identified reference states and quantified restoration potential. • High-suitability habitats exhibit both severe degradation and high potential. • Value-optimized scheme best balanced ecology and cost under resource constraints. In the face of accelerating biodiversity loss and ecosystem degradation, enhancing the effectiveness of ecological restoration under limited resources has become an urgent challenge. This study employed the snow leopard ( Panthera uncia ) as a case study to prioritize its restorable habitats through enhanced cost-effectiveness in the Sanjiangyuan region of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau. A multi-scale framework was developed to identify restoration priority areas by integrating habitat suitability, vegetation degradation, and vegetation restoration potential (VRP). The aim was to scientifically identify areas of high ecological value for restoration while minimizing costs. We used species distribution models to predict snow leopard habitats and applied the Mann-Kendall test and Sen’s Slope trend analysis to assess vegetation change trends. To estimate vegetation’s ideal ecological state, the counterfactual matching was used to calculate VRP by comparing it with current conditions. Systematic conservation planning was then employed to delineate core and general restoration areas. Results show 17.8% of suitable habitats exhibit significant vegetation degradation, with 68.6% located in medium to high suitability areas. High-VRP areas are mainly concentrated in the central and southern parts of the habitat, indicating high restoration value. The identified restoration priority areas cover 30% of the study area, with core areas comprising 64% of this subset. The proposed framework achieves over 60% coverage of areas with high suitability, severe degradation, and high VRP, demonstrating its potential for maximizing ecological benefits and optimizing resource allocation. This study provides a scientific foundation and practical framework for formulating targeted restoration strategies and enhancing endangered species conservation.

title: A framework for land use conflicts identification and zoning based on “scale-function-pattern”: Theory and application
abstract: • Construct a theoretical framework for LUCs based on “scale–function–pattern”. • Propose a multi-dimensional and multi-scale LUCs identification methodology. • Reveal spatiotemporal patterns of multi-dimensional LUCs in NSEBTM (2000–2020). • Define five zoning types to support sustainable land management. • Validate the new framework’s rationality and applicability. Land use conflicts (LUCs) represent the evolving interactions between human activities and land systems, posing critical challenges to sustainable land management. These conflicts typically manifest in mismatches of development scale, functional allocation, and spatial patterns. However, existing research often adopts single-dimensional or single-scale approaches, lacking a unified framework that integrates these key dimensions. To address this gap, we propose a multi-dimensional, multi-scale framework grounded in the “scale–function–pattern” paradigm. This framework systematically defines the conceptual connotations of LUCs, establishes identification methods, and develops zoning strategies by integrating a three-dimensional cube model and a triangular coordination model, supporting the delineation of conflict zones and targeted governance directions. Taking the Northern Slope Economic Belt of Tianshan Mountains (NSEBTM) as a case study, the results show that from 2000 to 2020, overall LUCs exhibited a declining trend, with higher conflict intensity in the west and lower in the east. Specifically: (1) Scale conflicts of land use significantly decreased, with severe cases mainly in developed but ecologically fragile areas; (2) Function conflicts of land use remained widespread but mild, with mild-conflict zones increasing from 51.08% to 76.27%; (3) Pattern conflicts of land use gradually declined, with moderate to severe cases concentrated in urbanized and rapidly urbanizing regions. Based on integrated classification, five zoning types were identified: key remediation zone (0.2%), functional optimization zone (52.75%), pattern adjustment zone, development regulation zone and strategic reserve zone. These findings offer a scientific basis for the coordinated management of LUCs and territorial spatial planning. This study deepens the understanding of LUCs from a multi-dimensional perspective and provides practical insights for sustainable land management.

title: Forest structural attributes as indicators and mediators of aboveground carbon storage and woody plant species richness in natural forests
abstract: • Tree carbon and species richness vary across six natural forest types in China. • Forest structure is a strong predictor of tree carbon and woody species richness. • Topsoil carbon is mainly shaped by environmental rather than structural variables. • Forest structure mediates the synergy between carbon storage and biodiversity. • Structural metrics can serve as indicators for multifunctional forest management. Understanding how forest structural attributes influence key ecosystem properties is essential for sustainable forest management. However, empirical evidence remains limited on whether forest structure can reliably indicate both carbon storage and biodiversity across diverse natural forest types. In this study, we examined six large forest dynamics plots representing major forest types in China to assess how forest structure and environmental conditions influence carbon storage in trees and woody plant species richness. Carbon storage in trees was estimated based on tree biomass, and woody species richness was derived from full tree inventories. We characterized forest structure using variation in tree diameter and height, stand basal area, and stem density. Our results show that forest structural complexity is a strong and consistent predictor of both carbon storage in trees and woody plant species richness across forest types. In contrast, topsoil carbon storage was primarily influenced by edaphic and environmental variables, with little association to forest structure. Moreover, we found that structural attributes not only independently influenced carbon and richness, but also mediated the positive relationship between them. These findings highlight forest structure as a robust, measurable, and management-relevant indicator of aboveground ecosystem functions and biodiversity. By identifying structural metrics that are sensitive to management and remotely observable, this study provides a basis for monitoring forest multifunctionality and integrating biodiversity and carbon goals into restoration and conservation planning across natural forest landscapes.

title: Analysis of the current status and future invasion trends of alien invasions on the Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau in the context of climate warming
abstract: The Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau, a globally critical biodiversity hotspot, faces increasing threats from climate change and human activities that raise the risk of alien species spread. However, the potential interactions of these factors, particularly in alpine zones, remain understudied. In this study, we used a species distribution model, incorporating multi-source data such as climate, altitude, and the Human Influence Index, to predict the potential distribution areas of 55 species listed in the List of State Key Managed Invasive Alien Species under current and projected climatic scenarios for the 2090 s. The results suggested that, under current climatic scenarios, invasive plants could potentially occupy 47.00 % of the Plateau, supporting the establishment of 27 species, while invasive animals might colonize 21.20 % of the area, enabling 15 species to persist. Factors related to human activities have a significant impact on model predictions, followed by those related to precipitation and temperature. Both human activities and climate variables affect species suitability. Under 2090 s-SSP5-8.5, invasive plants may occupy 57.00 % (+9.96 %) of the total area, with 29 species viable, and invasive animals may occupy 37.70 % (+16.43 %) of the total area, with 16 species viable. Our results also show that as the climate warms, the potential distribution areas are gradually expanding at mid-to-high altitudes. The optimum altitude is also likely shifting to mid-to-high altitude on the plateau, suggesting that alpine areas are increasingly at risk of invasion now and in the future. This study reveals the potential sensitivity of the Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau to invasive alien species and provides a scientific basis for managing invasive alien species.

title: Indicators of visual and ecological complexity of urban wetlands and lakes in Stockholm
abstract: • Visual and ecological complexity assessed via landscape and plant diversity data. • Edge contrast consistently predicted visual complexity across data sources. • Patch isolation effects differed between photo-based and orthophoto-based data sets. • Patch elongation is negatively associated with plant species diversity. • Findings suggest indicators of visual and ecological quality for urban planning. Recognising the aesthetic attributes of urban wetlands and lakes is crucial for guiding their sustainable management, as it fosters social motivation, which in turn contributes to the preservation of water ecosystems. Systematic assessments of landscape aesthetic quality based on visual indicators become essential for urban planning and design. This study focuses on the analysis of visual complexity as a key concept of the aesthetic quality of urban wetlands and lakes in the Stockholm area using indicators of visual quality. It also aims to enhance ecologically oriented landscape aesthetics by investigating how indicators of visual quality correlate with biodiversity parameters. The study employs landscape structure analysis combined with plant diversity analysis, applying a set of aerial photo-based and landscape photo-based indicators. The methodology used included GIS analysis of landscape photos and orthophotos, the identification of landscape metrics in FRAGSTATS, the selection of indices and visual indicators, plant species richness analysis, the evaluation of landscape structure using multivariate canonical analysis and assessment of the relationship between spatial landscape structure using mixed-effects modelling. The novelty of this study lies in introducing new indicators of visual complexity and in exploring the link between visual and ecological complexity in urban wetlands and lakes. The results showed: 1. that the analyzed canonical axes explained 17–50 % of the variation and were correlated with landscape metrics that serve as indicators of shape, aggregation, and edge contrast, suggesting that these metrics could be potential objective indicators of visual complexity; 2. that the effect of edge contrast was consistent but the effect of the index of patch isolation was different in different data sources; 3. and that patch elongation was negatively associated with Shannon diversity, suggesting that it is an integrative metric linking visual and ecological complexity. The results highlight the importance of integrating visual and ecological complexity indicators into monitoring programs and decision-making for managing urban green–blue infrastructure, promoting effective governance, preventing wetland degradation, and supporting participatory discussions for shared understanding.

title: Study on spatial synergy and identification of dual-disadvantage zones of healthcare facility equity and environmental health elements in Zhengzhou city
abstract: In the context of rapid urbanization, urban residents face challenges from both declining environmental quality and unequal healthcare resource distribution. This study examines Zhengzhou’s core urban area to explore the spatial relationship between key ecosystem services (urban cooling and air purification) and access to the highest tier of medical facilities (Grade A Class III hospitals), which are critical for handling severe and complex health conditions. Utilizing a robust framework combining InVEST model, the Gravity-based Two-Step Floating Catchment Area (G2SFCA) method, and bivariate spatial autocorrelation analysis, this research aims to unveil their spatial synergistic patterns and identify dual-disadvantage zones characterized by deficiencies in both environmental health elements and critical healthcare service supply. The findings reveal that urban ecosystem regulating services exhibit a gradient pattern, increasing from the urban core outwards, with the weakest provision within the Third Ring Road and the strongest beyond the Fourth Ring Road. Accessibility to Grade A Class III hospitals demonstrates a spatial pattern characterized by high levels within the Third Ring Road, weaker accessibility beyond this ring in the western, southern, and northern peripheries, and strong accessibility in the eastern areas. Equity in healthcare resource distribution is relatively high in traditional core districts such as Jinshui, while being severely deficient in emerging areas like Huiji and zones along the Third Ring Road. Through bivariate spatial autocorrelation and spatial matching analyses, the study identifies dual-disadvantage zones predominantly concentrated near the Third Ring Roads within Zhongyuan and Erqi. These zones concurrently face challenges of poor environmental quality and a scarcity of high-quality healthcare resources, thereby posing a dual threat to residents’ health and well-being. These findings hold significant theoretical and practical implications for enhancing healthcare resource allocation, promoting environmental justice, and improving environmental health management.

title: GeoRRDI: An explainable and multi-source data-driven framework for rural revitalization assessment with spatial heterogeneity consideration
abstract: • Proposed GeoRRDI, a multi-source and spatially interpretable framework. • Developed a four-dimensional, 19-indicator RRDI system with SHAP-based selection. • Designed a triple evaluation framework and identified the optimal GWRF-RF model. • Revealed spatial drivers and evolution through global–local importance and prediction. Current assessments of rural revitalization at the municipal scale and village-level granularity face persistent challenges, including limited data integration, weak spatial heterogeneity modeling, and unclear variable interaction mechanisms. These issues constrain the identification of development gaps and the design of targeted interventions. To address these challenges, this study proposes GeoRRDI (Geographically Explainable Rural Revitalization Development Index), an interpretable assessment framework integrating satellite-derived and multi-source geospatial data. Using 3093 administrative villages in Luoyang, Henan Province, China, as the study area, we construct a 19-indicator system across four dimensions: Ecological Conditions, Land Use Structure, Settlement Dynamics, and Service Accessibility. SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) is used to interpret variable importance and perform feature selection, enhancing the interpretability and applicability of the indicator system.
