Agricultural Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) does not explicitly assess ES; however, the potential benefits offered by an improved representation of agroecosystem processes reveal an urgent need for ES integration into LCA. Through a systematic review of scientific literature, we collected a list of methods applied to assess legumes ES in European conditions. Methods were grouped following the Common International Classification of Ecosystem Services (CICES) and through general ES definitions. At the end of the process, 148 methods were found, of which: 81.8% were associated with Regulation & Maintenance services; 8.1% to Provisioning services; and 10.1% described methods related to the combination of different CICES sections. No methods for Cultural services were found. Most of the methods were based on direct measurements, except for those ES already part of the current LCA frameworks. The Regulation & Maintenance section is the area with the most fragmented knowledge, with some ES presenting well-established methodologies (e.g. climate change buffering and leaching regulation) and others which are currently not fully integrated into LCA, such as biodiversity maintenance, pest control, and pollination. Future research should focus on LCA methodologies for the integration of emerging agriculture-related ES. Achieving more comprehensive LCA is necessary to improve the understanding of legumes’ role in maintaining agroecosystems functionality.

title: Remote but not isolated; an integrated ecosystem assessment across the marine ecosystem of the Azores
abstract: This study presents the first cross-sectoral Integrated Ecosystem Assessment (IEA) for the Azores archipelago, a remote mid-North Atlantic oceanic region. It identifies the diversity, interconnectedness, and implications of anthropogenic pressures on marine ecosystems, serving as a versatile tool to assess impact risk and ecosystem vulnerability. Drawing on a comprehensive literature review, expert judgment, and stakeholder engagement, the IEA evaluated 12 economic sectors, 16 pressures, and 28 ecological components across the nearly 1 million km² Azores Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ).The sectoral analysis revealed that fishing, tourism, and shipping collectively account for over 86% of the cumulative impact risk in the Azores EEZ. Among the various pressures, species extraction, bycatch, contaminants, invasive species, and marine litter alone contribute to 95% of the total impact risk on the region’s marine environment. Although coastal ecosystems represent just 1% of the EEZ, they bear more than 50% of the total impact risk—primarily affecting demersal fishes, elasmobranchs, and shallow/littoral rocky and reef habitats. Other highly vulnerable components include pelagic and deep-sea elasmobranchs, marine mammals, and seabirds.The study also underscores critical knowledge gaps, with 50% of impact chains relying on global data due to a lack of region-specific evidence—particularly in deep-sea and abyssal ecosystems. This IEA provides essential insights for Ecosystem-Based Management (EBM), aligning regional monitoring priorities with the requirements of EU marine conservation and spatial planning directives.

title: Liana removal alters canopy chemistry more than structure in tropical seasonal forests: Insights from UAV-borne hyperspectral and LiDAR data
abstract: The abundance of lianas (woody vines) has increased in tropical forests due to climate change and fragmentation, altering important ecosystem functions related to both carbon and water cycles. The quantification and mapping of lianas’ effects on the forest canopy are therefore needed, yet they remain unresolved. This study investigates the effects of liana removal on the chemical and structural properties of the canopy in a tropical seasonal semideciduous forest in São Paulo, Brazil, using multitemporal UAV-borne hyperspectral (400–1000 nm) and LiDAR data. The study leveraged 18 plots (each 45 × 44 m; 0.198 ha), comprising 12 liana removal plots and 6 unmanaged controls, surveyed in both dry and wet seasons. In the dry season, pigment-sensitive vegetation indices (e.g., PARS, GMI1, SR3) showed medium to large negative responses to removal, reflecting reduced canopy greenness as evergreen lianas, sustained by deep roots, dominate amid tree defoliation. Conversely, wet-season indices (e.g., DD, OSAVI2, MSAVI) exhibited negligible effects, with resource abundance masking differences. LiDAR metrics revealed small to medium reductions in leaf area index (LAI), especially understory LAI, and increased gap fraction variability post-removal, with stronger contrasts during the dry season. These findings highlight UAV remote sensing’s potential for detailed, seasonal monitoring of liana influences on canopy chemistry and structure, informing targeted management to enhance forest resilience in varying tropical environments.

title: Visual perception of retaining walls in mountainous landscapes: an aesthetic quality assessment of post-earthquake geohazard prevention projects in Jiuzhaigou, China
abstract: Architectural aesthetics are an indispensable part of urban communities, closely related to human experience and well-being. However, in mountainous natural landscapes, the aesthetic quality of retaining walls is often overlooked, despite their potential discordance or even conflict with the natural scenery. This study integrates the morphological parameters of retaining walls (including color, lines, scale, etc.) before and after ecological interventions with tourists' perceptions to assess the scenic beauty estimation (SBE) of large-scale retaining walls post-earthquake in Jiuzhaigou. The results indicate that enhancing vegetation coverage on the external space of retaining walls and reducing the color distance between retaining walls and surrounding forests can significantly improve their visual integration with the landscape. The overall aesthetic perception of the evaluators tends to be consistent, with ecologically treated walls 8b, 6b, and 9b appearing more natural and having stronger visual beauty. Additionally, the transformation of the top shape and positioning of retaining walls is considered a key factor in increasing SBE. The study emphasizes the importance of adaptive and environmentally sensitive designing strategies for ecologically treating retaining walls of different locations and scales. Overall, this research demonstrates that enhancing the coordination of the structural form and color of retaining walls with the natural environment can effectively reduce visual impact and even enhance the aesthetic experience of different demographic groups. This study provides significant architectural aesthetic theory and practical insights for geohazard mitigation projects in nature reserves and scenic spots.

title: Research on the primary production required (PPR) supporting China’s freshwater aquaculture system—from the perspective of producing edible crude protein
abstract: As the world’s largest producer, China’s aquaculture plays a pivotal role in global aquatic food systems. The primary production required (PPR) metric is crucial for evaluating the ecological efficiency of protein production. This study presents the first comprehensive account of PPR for China’s freshwater aquaculture animals (FAA) from 2003 to 2023, focusing on edible crude protein (ECP) output. We introduced two novel efficiency parameters: PPR per unit wet weight and, more importantly, PPR per unit ECP. Results reveal a 59.35 % surge in total PPR, reaching 1.432 × 10 8 t-C in 2023. Strikingly, this PPR represented 262.54 % of the net primary production (NPP) of all Chinese lakes, reservoirs, and ponds, indicating a massive ’ecological deficit’. Nationally, it accounted for 4.475 % of terrestrial NPP, and globally, for 0.235 % of combined agricultural and marine NPP. Concurrently, the PPR intensity per ECP unit grew by 32.65 % (1.55 % annually), signaling a decline in ecological efficiency driven by a shift towards high-trophic species (e.g., bass, crayfish). Despite this, China’s FAA systems maintained a lower mean trophic level (3.13) than global wild fisheries (4.12), highlighting a comparative efficiency within the PPR framework. Our findings underscore that China’s aquaculture growth is increasingly reliant on external feed inputs, displacing environmental pressure onto global ecosystems. The study provides critical insights and strategic pathways for China’s blue transformation, emphasizing the need to prioritize low-PPR/ECP species for sustainable development.

title: From stand-scale palaeoecology to the conservation of old-growth ‘ancient’ woodland
abstract: • A novel multi-proxy palaeoecological approach to woodland dynamics and management. • The resilience of high conservation value woodlands with long legacies of human impact. • Maps and ancient woodland indicators may inaccurately identify ancient woodlands. Linkages between woodland longevity and conservation value are often assumed but rarely tested. The superiority of ‘old growth’ or ‘ancient’ woodlands for biodiversity and carbon sequestration is being increasingly recognised, yet deterioration is ongoing. There is a need to better understand and reliably identify ‘ancient’ woodlands to appropriately protect their conservation value. Maps, toponymics and ancient woodland indicator species can provide conflicting, potentially unreliable, evidence of woodland longevity. This research aims to demonstrate how palaeoecological indicators can be tailored to provide vital linkages between long-term palaeoecology and short-term ecology for understanding woodland history and informing management of valuable habitats. We apply a multi-indicator approach of stand-scale analyses of pollen, non-pollen palynomorphs, loss-on-ignition, charcoal and plant macrofossils to address uncertainties in woodland antiquity and explore disturbance dynamics. Our approach validates the status of ‘ancient’ woodlands, highlighting their longevity and co-evolved features of conservation value, and the need for cautious interpretation of alternative indicators of woodland history. We identify substantial compositional and structural changes where woodland has persisted for over 3500 years, and resilience to external forcings, including fire, herbivory, climatic changes and people. We demonstrate the need to integrate tailored palaeoecological indicators into modern woodland management to identify appropriate management strategies, including re-diversifying tree species composition and reinstating sustainable disturbance regimes. Of broader significance, how we define ‘ancient’ woodlands requires reconsideration in light of potential inaccuracies in alternative evidence of woodland longevity, and the unique histories that have shaped ancient woodlands requires recognition, which can all be realised using palaeoecological indicators.

title: Soil multifunctionality in arid mining: Driving mechanisms and restoration strategies based on natural succession
abstract: Ecological restoration in coal mining areas often relies mainly on artificial intervention. Restoration efficiency and long-term maintenance of soil multifunctionality remain limited due to an insufficient understanding of natural succession mechanisms. To clarify the patterns and driving mechanisms of soil multifunctionality in different succession types, this study used natural succession (NS) as an ecological reference, comparing changes in soil carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus multifunctionality between artificially restored (AR) and NS. Also explored how microbial communities and environmental factors influence these processes. The results indicated that soil multifunctionality increased significantly during the succession. Bacterial diversity responded more strongly to succession than fungal diversity. Employing multi-threshold and averaging methods, we found bacterial abundance positively influenced multifunctionality in AR (R med : 3.834 to 11.035, R 2 : 0.37 to 0.60) but negatively influenced multifunctionality in NS (R med : -5.926 to -3.304, R 2 : 0.17 to 0.25). Microbial community composition, rather than diversity alone, was identified as the key factor explaining multifunctionality. In AR, multifunctionality was mainly regulated by keystone bacteria and fungi. In NS, it was co-driven by keystone and rare bacterial taxa. While there was no significant correlation between fungal diversity and multifunctionality, certain keystone fungal phyla in AR (Ascomycota, Basidiomycota, and Chytridiomycota) have a significant influence on multifunctionality. Soil physical structure and water-salinity properties explained multifunctionality better than microbial factors. This suggests that improving the abiotic environment was more effective for promoting functional recovery than focusing only on microbial diversity. The study proposes a reclamation strategy of “structure-first and stage-progression” using NS as an ecological template to guide mining restoration. This strategy emphasizes the importance of synergistically optimizing environmental and biological elements.

title: Aerosol optical depth and ozone enhance their impacts on vegetation productivity via temperature in urban agglomerations of China
abstract: • How multiple factors influence vegetation productivity in urban and non-urban areas. • Used a spatial analysis model to capture spatial heterogeneity of vegetation productivity. • Path analysis revealed the pathways influencing vegetation productivity. • Aerosols and ozone affect vegetation productivity through temperature in urban agglomerations. Vegetation growth is closely linked to human well-being and is essential for maintaining ecological balance and enhancing biodiversity. Given the rapid urbanization, exploring how climate and environmental pollution influence vegetation gross primary production (GPP) in China is essential. Vegetation GPP, temperature, precipitation, aerosol optical depth (AOD), CO 2 emissions, and O 3 data from 2001 to 2023 were analysed. By applying Theil–Sen trend analysis, a Geographically and Temporally Weighted Regression (GTWR) model, and path analysis, the spatiotemporal evolution of vegetation GPP in Chinese urban and nonurban agglomerations and its response to environmental factors were explored. The findings revealed considerable vegetation GPP increases in 67.15% of the study area. The total vegetation GPP and its growth rate in urban agglomerations were notably greater than those in nonurban agglomerations. While most urban agglomerations will continue to grow, certain coastal regions will face greater degradation risks. AOD showed a negative correlation on vegetation GPP in some coastal urban agglomerations, while its negative correlation was weakened in the northeastern urban agglomerations. O 3 showed a positive correlation on vegetation GPP in the coastal urban agglomerations. With temperature as an indirect factor, AOD and O 3 promote vegetation GPP changes, with three to five times greater intensities in urban agglomerations than in nonurban agglomerations. Precipitation is the primary driver of vegetation GPP increase in nonurban agglomerations but yields negative effects in humid coastal urban agglomerations, highlighting the multifactor pollution stress–climate compensation–vegetation response coupling mechanism. This study aimed to provide insights into multiscale ecosystem interactions and differentiated management strategies under urbanization.

title: Towards a generalisation of the spatial species mingling diversity index
abstract: Species diversity is an important notion of all ecosystems and much contributes to its inner functioning. Currently biodiversity is threatened by global changes including climate change. Spatial species mingling is a refinement of species diversity considering how individual plants of varying species are spatially mixed with those of others in local neighbourhoods. An important objective of conservation is to halt or at least to retard species diversity loss. A key element of monitoring systems, which can establish imminent threats to species, are reliable indices quantifying diversity. In this study, we proposed a generalised spatial species mingling index for an improved monitoring of how individual plants of certain species spatially mix with those of other species. A key feature of our new concept is a devaluation of instances of species inequality caused by recurrent neighbour species. The devaluation uses a memory function and is derived from proportional rules in multiwinner approval voting of political science. Our detailed analysis revealed that our new species mingling index has several statistical advantages over previous index concepts and is ecologically more plausible. Whilst dealing efficiently with recurrent species among the nearest neighbours, the new index is less dependent on global and local species richness than previous indices. Additionally, the index allows for adjustments by a parameter which can freely be chosen. Based on our analysis we recommend the use of our generalised species mingling index in the monitoring of spatial species diversity.

title: Taxonomic and functional diversity reveal contrasting crab community dynamics under artificial and natural pond to mangrove restoration
abstract: • Compared crab taxonomic and functional diversity across 27-year restoration chronosequence. • Artificial restoration promoted rapid early colonization but later converged with natural sites. • Community succession shifted from filter-feeding Ocypodidae to herbivorous-omnivorous Grapsoidea. • Naturally restored sites showed functional group composition closer to natural mangroves. • Soil pH and salinity were key drivers of crab community taxonomic and functional patterns. Mangrove restoration is critical for the resilience of coastal ecosystems, yet there remains insufficient research on the ecological effects of artificial versus natural restoration, especially regarding their impacts on faunal communities and ecosystem functions. This study used a space-for-time substitution approach to investigate the taxonomic and functional diversity of crab communities along a 27-year pond-to-mangrove restoration chronosequence in Dongzhaigang Bay, southern China. We analyzed temporal changes in community composition and functional traits under artificial and natural restoration approaches, compared alpha diversity and the components of beta diversity across sites, and explored the influence of environmental variables on variations in crab community structure. A total of 3,700 crabs representing 24 species were recorded. Artificial restoration sites exhibited rapid early colonization, with species richness reaching 1.5 times that of natural restoration sites by year 4. However, by year 27, both artificial and natural restoration sites showed no significant differences in crab taxonomic and functional diversity compared to natural mangroves. The results indicate that species composition in both restoration types underwent a typical successional process, beginning with dominance by filter-feeding Ocypodidae crabs in the early stages and gradually shifting to dominance by herbivorous and omnivorous crabs of the Grapsoidea family in later stages. Nevertheless, the proportion of functional groups in naturally restored sites was closer to that of natural mangroves. Soil pH and salinity were identified as the primary environmental drivers shaping both taxonomic and functional community patterns. Based on these findings, we emphasize the importance of incorporating functional traits and successional dynamics alongside taxonomic metrics to more accurately assess the ecological recovery of mangrove restoration efforts.

title: Enhancing Natura 2000 habitat monitoring: A framework for biodiversity conservation assessment
abstract: Habitat monitoring and conservation assessment have gained importance in the EU, especially since the adoption of the Habitats Directive and the creation of the Natura 2000 network. Accurate reporting on habitat conservation status depends on detailed knowledge of habitat distribution. Advances in open-access biodiversity databases, remote sensing, and artificial intelligence have improved ecosystem mapping, while field surveys remain essential for understanding habitat dynamics.This study proposes a standardized framework for habitat mapping and monitoring, applied in the Latium region of Central Italy. A large dataset of georeferenced vegetation plots was collected through systematic fieldwork. Using expert system classification and clustering analysis, each plot was assigned to a habitat type defined in Annex I of the Habitats Directive (92/43/EEC). These labeled plots were then used to train Habitat Distribution Models based on Random Forest algorithms, generating high-resolution habitat maps.The maps were refined through probability thresholding and validated using the Article 17 reporting dataset, primarily based on expert judgment. The methodology successfully identified 41 habitat types, including coastal, dune, grassland, rocky, and forest ecosystems. This approach provides a reproducible and scalable workflow that supports regional and national conservation reporting. It delivers robust spatial data on habitat distribution, contributing to more effective conservation strategies, improved long-term monitoring, and better-informed ecological restoration actions.

title: Multimodal remote sensing and meteorological estimation of long-term spatial-scale non-point source pollution in inland reservoir
abstract: • Multimodal model of remote sensing imagery, meteorological data and lag effects. • 30-year, spatial assessment of NPS pollution across 7 water quality parameters. • Multimodal models achieved higher accuracy and broader parameter estimation. • Meteorological lag effects greatly enhanced model accuracy and interpretability. Non-point source (NPS) pollution is one of the major threats to inland waters. This issue is particularly pronounced in remote regions, where the scarcity of long-term and spatial-scale water quality data hampers effective NPS pollution assessment. This study selected Chitian Reservoir, a tropical drinking water source, as a case study. A total of 323 samples were obtained from 2021 to 2023. Water quality observations were used as labels, and Landsat imagery together with meteorological factors with up to a two-day lag were used as input features. Based on four machine learning algorithms, multimodal water quality models with both spatial and temporal attributes were developed. Results showed that the multimodal models effectively estimated the concentrations of multiple water quality parameters, including total nitrogen (TN), total phosphorus (TP), ammonium nitrogen (AN), chlorophyll-a (CA), permanganate index (PI), total suspended substance (TSS), and turbidity (TU), achieving R 2 values of 0.71, 0.50, 0.70, 0.53, 0.83, 0.80 and 0.65, respectively, on the test set. Compared to unimodal models based on either remote sensing or meteorological factors, the multimodal models could estimate 3–4 additional water quality parameters, with accuracy improvements ranging from 2.01% to 63.80%. SHAP analysis revealed that spectral bands and lagged meteorological factors contributed significantly to the estimation of water quality parameters. When the models were extended to the period from 1994 to 2023, the spatiotemporal characteristics of water quality parameters exhibited significant differences. AN and TSS concentrations were higher in nearshore areas, while other parameters were higher in central zones. TP showed a clear declining trend, whereas other parameters remained relatively stable over the three decades. Concentrations of TP, AN, PI, TSS, and TU showed significantly higher during the rainy season, while TN exhibited the opposite trend. The proposed multimodal water quality model substantially improved both the number and estimation accuracy of water quality parameters. It identified the sensitive areas and key periods of NPS pollution in Chitian Reservoir across multiple dimensions, including a 30-year temporal span, spatial distribution, and multiple water quality parameters. These findings provide scientific support for water environment management in the study watershed and offer a valuable technical reference for long-term, spatial-scale, and multi-parameter water quality monitoring and NPS pollution control worldwide.

title: Moso bamboo (Phyllostachys edulis) expansion drives divergent mycorrhizal responses and stand reorganization via soil nitrogen and phosphorus imbalance and microbial network restructuring
abstract: • Moso bamboo differentially regulates mycorrhizae in L. chinense and S. japonica . • It simplified L. chinense ’s microbial network but enhanced complexity for S. japonica. • Our model shows bamboo affects plants via nutrients and microbes (63% indirect effect). Moso bamboo ( Phyllostachys edulis ) expansion into adjacent forests reduces plant diversity and disrupts soil nutrient cycling. However, the ecological mechanisms through which it drives stand simplification via soil-microbe-plant system interactions remain systematically unexplored. To unravel these mechanisms, we investigated different stand layers along an expansion gradient from pure moso bamboo forests to coniferous-broadleaved mixed forests from a soil-microbe-plant perspective. Results showed that moso bamboo expansion significantly altered soil nitrogen and phosphorus distributions, with a 56.8 % increase in ammonium nitrogen, a 36.3 % decrease in nitrate nitrogen, and a 46.3 % decrease in available phosphorus. These changes enhanced the competitive advantage of bamboo and Serissa japonica in the regeneration layer but suppressed Loropetalum chinense in the succession layer. Expansion reduced the mycorrhizal colonization rate of L. chinense by 24.04 %, accompanied by a decline in the abundance of mycorrhizal fungi such as Oidiodendron . Conversely, S. japonica exhibited a 9.9 % increase in mycorrhizal colonization, along with greater microbial network complexity and functionality. Partial least squares structural equation modeling indicated that expansion indirectly suppressed mycorrhizal colonization and abundance of L. chinense and promoted those of S. japonica by altering soil nitrogen-phosphorus balance and beneficial microbe abundance (indirect effect > 64.3 %), with mycorrhizal colonization being the key pathway ( β > 0.925). Overall, moso bamboo expansion drives stand restructuring by differentially affecting plant-mycorrhizal interactions via soil nutrient redistribution and microbial community reassembly. These findings provide a novel theoretical framework for managing bamboo expansion and promoting sustainable forest management.

title: Optimization of the National Ecological Observatory Network root sampling design
abstract: The design of the National Ecological Observatory Network (NEON) was informed by literature review, consultation with subject matter experts, and analysis of prototype data collection efforts. To ensure long-term scientific validity and resource efficiency, we analyzed multiple years of continental-scale NEON data collected according to the initial design to determine whether it was possible to fine-tune the time-intensive root sampling protocol to optimize resources while still meeting initial design requirements. We focused our analyses on field sampling (since the number of cores collected has a significant impact on time-intensive laboratory sorting) and laboratory dilution sampling for fine root fragments. Using bootstrapping and power analysis methods we determined that there were 8 (out of 47) terrestrial sites where we could reduce within-plot replication in field sampling and still detect change in fine root biomass in a pooled 0–2 mm size category, and we implemented this in early 2025. Furthermore, we used a combination of bootstrapping and temporal change analysis methods to determine that lab subsampling procedures to estimate fine root fragment biomass could be reduced from 10 to 3 subsample replicates at all 47 terrestrial NEON sites without adversely impacting the ability to estimate total fine root biomass, and we implemented this change in early 2024. In combination, these analyses allowed us to reduce labor requirements for two components of the NEON root sampling protocol while still delivering high quality open-source data available to all users at https://data.neonscience.org/data-products/DP1.10067.001 .

title: Considering parameter seasonal variation to enhance process-based ecosystem model performance, evidence from the SWH model
abstract: • Empirical parameters in the SWH models effectively characterize evapotranspiration dynamics. • Introducing temporal dynamics into parameter calibration scheme enhanced model predictive accuracy. • Improved Monte Carlo-based calibration scheme significantly enhanced model performance. Modeling and partitioning ecosystem evapotranspiration (ET) are critical for predicting how ecosystem water cycles respond to global climate change. In this study, we used the widely applied SWH model, an ET partitioning model, as an example. We demonstrated that certain empirical calibrated parameters (e.g., scaling coefficients used in the calculation of surface soil resistance and canopy stomatal resistance) can effectively characterize ET states, as evidenced by global FLUXNET data. These parameters showed distinct discrepancy across ecosystem types, and exhibited strong correlations with climatic factors such as precipitation, soil moisture and temperature. However, existing studies often assume these parameters to be temporally constant, which limits the model’s ability to capture seasonal ET dynamics. To address this, we developed a series of parameter calibration schemes by adjusting parameters within adaptive time windows (L), which allow parameters to vary temporally. Results showed that for ecosystems with pronounced seasonal dynamics, such as savannas and temperate forests, the length of L aligns well with the specific seasonal characteristics. The improved Monte Carlo-based calibration scheme achieved a 95% success rate, with R 2 significantly higher than traditional strategy (10–30% improvement). At 20 long-term observation sites, its performance approached that of the Extended Kalman Filtering (EKF), which yielded R 2 values between 0.83 and 0.98.​ This calibration scheme is sound in theory and easy to apply in practice, and would enhance the capability of similar models in simulating ET dynamics. Future studies should pay more attention to the temporal variability of parameters to more accurately capture specific ecosystem indicators and enhance predictive capacity.

title: Acoustic detection of a nocturnal bird with deep learning: the challenge of low signal-to-noise ratio
abstract: Automatic sound classification is a promising approach to analyze the spatio-temporal dynamics of natural sound sources. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have proved to be particularly effective for the classification of animal sounds. However, even if these algorithms are more efficient than their predecessors, CNNs need to show stable performances despite various sources of variability. The signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) has been identified in the literature as a key parameter in the performance of sound classification algorithms. In this study, we investigated the influence of the SNR during the training and inference of a custom-built CNN for the mono-specific classification of Boreal Owl ( Aegolius funereus ) vocalizations. The repetitive, stereotyped nocturnal vocalizations of this species are ideal for isolating the effects of the SNR. Experiments showed that even if the custom-built model was trained with very low SNRs, it still very poorly detected low SNR vocalizations during testing. Performance drops per SNR of the custom-built model were comparable to those of the popular model BirdNET. If the custom-built model outperformed BirdNET overall, both models seemed to have similar performance drops as soon as vocalizations had a SNR inferior to 3 dB. Finally, the custom-built model classified 6 years of audio recordings from 4 autonomous recorders in the Risoux forest (France) and highlighted the variations in the Boreal Owl vocalization activity on a yearly, monthly and hourly scale.

title: Evaluating the predictability of SIF at multiple temporal scales for winter wheat yield in Huang-Huai-Hai plain
abstract: As a remote sensing indicator of vegetation physiology, solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (SIF) serves as a proxy for photosynthesis and has been widely used for monitoring stress conditions such as drought and for estimating crop yields. However, few studies systematically evaluated the capacity of SIF to indicate crop yield variations under drought and non-drought conditions across different temporal scales. This study focused on the Huang-Huai-Hai Plain (HHHP) and used the Standardized Soil Moisture Index (SSMI) to identify the spatial distribution of agricultural drought. We compared the sensitivity of SIF740, SIF683, NDVI, and NIRv to drought during different growth stages of winter wheat, and examined the associations between SIF740 and winter wheat yield under drought and non-drought conditions at various temporal scales. The results indicated that SIF740 was more sensitive to drought than SIF683, NDVI, and NIRv, particularly during the regreening stage. Under non-drought conditions, cumulative SIF740 during the jointing-anthesis stage exhibited the strongest correlation with winter wheat yield, outperforming instantaneous and growing-season scale estimates. Under drought conditions, the association between SIF740 and yield improved with increasing temporal scale, with seasonal cumulative SIF740 showing the best performance. This study further elucidated the underlying mechanisms of the association between SIF and crop yield, providing a representative example for SIF-based regional yield estimation.

title: Layering for governance: Ecosystem service supply–demand trade-offs and social-ecological system network topologies from a cluster perspective
abstract: A key challenge in ensuring the coordinated development of ecological conservation and economic growth is to gain a solid understanding of the interactions between supply–demand of ecosystem services (ES). However, empirical research on spatial imbalance among ESs and its interrelationships remain scarce, especially regarding its bidirectional network topology with ecological-social elements. Here, ecosystem service supply–demand rate (ES-SDR) was assessed in the Mulan River basin, one of the birthplaces of China’s modern ecological civilization ideology, and four bundles of supply–demand rate for ecosystem services (BSDRES) were constructed. The study hierarchically identified global and local ES-SDR trade-offs/synergies and identified core of ES-SDR connections by constructing the Hub-ES index. Finally, established a comprehensive ecological-social coupling network and hierarchically identified the dominant factors of ES-SDR trade-offs/synergies using redundancy analysis. Results reveal that nearly all ES-SDRs exhibit a gradient transition from surplus (northwest) to deficit (southeast), forming four BSDRES Ⅰ–Ⅳ, highlighting diverse imbalances. From global and local perspectives in different bundles, the spatial heterogeneity of trade-off/synergy relationships was identified, with carbon supply–demand relationships losing central role, while water supply–demand relationships becoming hub. Additionally, the network established between these relationships and ecological-social factors reveals that land use/cover change (LUCC) plays a critical hub function in coupled system, dominating multi-factor interaction and transmission. Trade-off/synergy of ES-SDR are mostly distributed around LUCC and become key transmission medium. Across different bundles, population density has the highest explanatory power for ES-SDR trade-off/synergy. Overall, our research provides novel insights into the emerging attributes and complexity of these supply–demand relationships.

title: The times they are a changin’: Temporal patterns in small cetacean abundance in the northeast Atlantic
abstract: • Abundance of 7 cetacean species in the NE Atlantic was estimated using aerial surveys. • Seasonal and interannual fluctuations in abundance were reported. • Harbour porpoise abundance decrease suggests a population decline in Irish waters. • Changes in bottlenose dolphin abundance may reflect movements in NE Atlantic. • Common dolphin abundance changes may reflect broad scale movements in N Atlantic. Conserving marine species effectively requires spatially and temporally explicit knowledge of their abundance and distribution for assessing potential impacts (e.g., from fishery bycatch, anthropogenic sound, ship strikes) over different spatial and temporal scales. We used aerial surveys and distance sampling to estimate abundance of seven frequently encountered small cetacean species in the northeast Atlantic and examine seasonal and interannual variations. Five surveys were carried out over the Irish EEZ in summer 2016, 2021 and 2022 and winter 2016–2017 and 2022–2023. Seasonal and annual variations in abundance were seen across species. Harbour porpoise showed a steady decrease in abundance, with estimates ranging from 38,260 (CV: 23.7) individuals in summer 2016 to 6,604 (CV: 40.8) in winter 2022–2023. Similarly, bottlenose dolphin numbers ranged from an unprecedented 212,646 (CV: 15.5) individuals in the winter of 2016–2017 to 11,328 (CV: 42.4) in summer 2021. In contrast, common dolphins increased from 13,192 (CV: 75.2) individuals in winter 2016–2017 to 594,293 (CV: 28.2) in summer 2021. Other species, such as Risso’s, Atlantic white-sided, white-beaked and striped dolphins were seen more sporadically and in lower numbers. The recent decline in harbour porpoise abundance is concerning and merits further investigation. Results provide the first measure of seasonal and interannual variability in abundance, possibly reflecting large scale movement patterns and population change and allow for the seasonal assessment of potential anthropogenic impacts.

title: Exploring the dynamic relationships and mechanisms driving a long-term sequence of ecosystem services in mountains based on ecosystem service bundles
abstract: Mountain ecosystems are typical fragile ecological systems that face severe challenges in providing ecosystem services (ES) due to the dual pressures of global climate change and intensified human activities. However, there is limited research on the long-term spatiotemporal dynamics and driving mechanisms of ES in mountainous regions. The Wuling Mountain Area (WMA) is a key ecological function zone in central China, and plays a critical role in maintaining regional ecological security and promoting sustainable development through its stable supply of ES. Using long-term data from 2000 to 2020, this study first assessed the spatiotemporal characteristics and variations for four key ES in WMA: habitat quality (HQ), net primary productivity (NPP), soil conservation (SC), and water yield (WY). Then, the K-means clustering method was used to identify ecosystem service bundles (ESB). A Pearson correlation analysis and the XGBoost model were applied to explore trade-offs and synergies among ES and their driving mechanisms, respectively. The results indicate the following. (1) ES in WMA exhibited significant spatial heterogeneity. HQ showed a slight downward trend (slope = -0.002), while NPP (slope = 2.19), SC (slope = 1.17), and WY (slope = 5.39) all showed increasing trends. (2) There were four types of ESB: Core Ecological Bundle (CEB, 28.20%), Water Abundance Bundle (WAB, 21.66%), Balanced Production Bundle (BPB, 28.16%), and Ecological Transition Bundle (ETB, 21.98%). Each had distinct dominant services and spatial distributions. (3) Relationships among ES varied dynamically, with HQ generally showing trade-offs with NPP, SC, and WY. In contrast, NPP-SC, NPP-WY, and SC-WY mostly displayed synergistic relationships. These relationships also varied significantly across different ESB. (4) Both natural and socio-economic drivers jointly influenced ES changes, often with nonlinear threshold effects. For example, HQ declined markedly in CEB when the proportion of cropland area exceeded 14%. Based on these findings, the study proposes different management strategies for different ESB, providing scientific support for functional zoning and sustainable development in the WMA.

title: Assessing the environmental status of cold-water coral reefs: BARCS, a novel multi-parametric index
abstract: Cold-water coral (CWC) frameworks are complex biogenic structures that sustain high biodiversity and provide essential ecosystem services in the deep sea. These vulnerable ecosystems are increasingly threatened by anthropogenic activities, particularly bottom fishing. While much research has addressed the origin, distribution, and ecology of CWC reefs, little attention has been devoted to the standardised assessment of their conservation status. Within the European Union, the Marine Strategy Framework Directive (MSFD) requires member states to evaluate the environmental status of marine ecosystems. However, monitoring efforts largely focus on coastal waters, with limited initiatives targeting the deep sea. Here, we present the BAthyal coral Reefs Conservation Status (BARCS) index, a multi-parametric tool designed to evaluate and monitor deep-sea scleractinian-dominated ecosystems. The BARCS index integrates two components: a Structure Index (SI), which assesses reef complexity, demographic parameters of habitat-forming scleractinians, and associated species richness; and an Impact Index (II), which quantifies anthropogenic pressure based on sedimentation, marine litter, and entanglement. Together, these yield ten metrics that can be reliably derived from remotely operated vehicle (ROV) footage. The index was tested at eleven Mediterranean sites (across the Gulf of Lions and Ligurian, Tyrrhenian, Ionian, and Adriatic seas), encompassing diverse ecological settings and levels of human impact. Results demonstrate its ability to discriminate among environmental conditions and to disentangle natural variability from anthropogenic stressors. Validation against independent proxies of human impact further supports its robustness. The BARCS index thus represents the first standardised tool for assessing and monitoring bathyal CWC reefs in line with MSFD requirements.

title: Corrigendum to “Integrating multi-temporal information for monitoring plant spectral diversity with PlanetScope and Sentinel-2 satellite imagery”. [Ecol. Indic. 180 (2025) 114348]
Beyond mean trait distance: An integrated approach to functional distinctiveness
abstract: • Functional distinctiveness is a key concept in ecology, reflecting the extent to which a species exhibits unique functional traits. • We propose a novel framework that links functional distinctiveness to rarity functions, a fundamental component of diversity measures. • We apply this approach to examine changes in functional distinctiveness along an Alpine plant succession. • Our results highlight the importance of integrating distinctiveness and rarity functions to fully capture the ecological roles of functionally distinct species. Functional distinctiveness is a key concept in ecology, reflecting the extent to which a species exhibits unique functional traits relative to other species in the assemblage. While functionally distinct species often contribute disproportionately to ecosystem processes, their role in shaping community functioning remains underexplored. In this study, we propose an integrated framework that links functional distinctiveness to rarity functions, a fundamental component of diversity measures, thereby generalizing distinctiveness metrics beyond the simple calculation of mean trait distance. The main advantage of the proposed framework lies in its ability to adjust the sensitivity of distinctiveness to changes in the abundance of rare or common species, thus providing a more accurate representation of community structure. We apply this approach to an Alpine plant succession, examining changes in functional distinctiveness across six successional stages. Our results reveal a gradual decline in functional diversity along the succession, driven by a progressive reduction in the functional distinctiveness of the most abundant species within plots. Additionally, we demonstrate that measures of functional distinctiveness that are more sensitive to rare species provide a more refined understanding of changes in the functional structure of communities during succession. This study highlights the importance of integrating distinctiveness and rarity functions to better capture the ecological roles of functionally distinct species and inform biodiversity conservation strategies.

title: Evaluating coastal multifunctionality: Sand nourishment strategies at decadal scales
abstract: Globally, there is a growing societal need for multifunctional coastal climate adaptation of sandy shores in the coming decades. Sand nourishment strategies are increasingly regarded as promising nature-based approaches to adaptation. They may increase flood safety and mitigate coastal erosion while enhancing recreational and ecological functioning. However, their multifunctional potential has not yet been assessed under diverse climate impacts at decadal scales. This study analysed the effects of beach, shoreface and mega-nourishment strategies on the physical capacity of sandy shores to supply coastal multifunctionality, using a systems-based approach. Through a structured literature review, we identified eight indicators for recreational (2 indicators), ecological (3) and flood safety (3) functions. We integrated these indicators into a process-based sand distribution model for dissipative coastal profiles. We simulated indicator states as the coastal profile responded to the nourishment strategies under five sea-level rise scenarios and three erosion rates. Next, we calculated the extent to which the physical capacity for coastal functions and multifunctionality were supplied over six decades. Our results indicate that all three nourishment strategies can highly supply the capacity for coastal multifunctionality, although the drivers of this potential differed per strategy. These findings imply that sand nourishment strategies are viable approaches for multifunctional coastal climate adaptation in the coming decades. However, they require prioritising specific coastal features and functions. Although sand nourishment strategies remain high-impact interventions, they also allow for intentionally creating coastal landscapes. These landscapes may not only provide flood protection but also enhance the specific environmental and societal functions valued in dissipative sandy shores. Prioritising among these functions requires explicit political choices

title: Deriving exploratory temperature-based phenological indicators under data-limited conditions: integrating ERA5 and citizen science
abstract: Understanding phenological responses to temperature variability in tropical and subtropical systems remains a major research gap, hindered by the scarcity of long-term observational datasets. We present an exploratory workflow that integrates temperature indicators derived from ERA5-Land reanalysis with opportunistic flowering records from citizen science to predict the onset of flowering in Crateva religiosa, a geographically widespread yet understudied tropical-subtropical deciduous tree species. Using partial least squares (PLS) regression on 93 opportunistic citizen science records, we identified potential thermal indicators, including low-percentile temperatures and long-window variability metrics, that together explained 71.18% of the variation in flowering date (RMSE = 12.13 days). Our findings highlight the potential thermal sensitivity signals of C. religiosa and demonstrate that biologically informed indicators can extract potential predictive value from coarse-resolution and noisy datasets. This approach illustrates a pragmatic workflow for deriving exploratory phenological variables in data-limited regions. It may serve as a valuable entry point for biodiversity monitoring, climate impact assessments, and early-stage evaluation of phenological sensitivity in understudied non-model species.
